## DAILY SECURITY BRIEFING

### 1. Russia launches major missile and drone attack on Kyiv
Russia attacked Kyiv and its surrounding region with 168 drones and dozens of cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles. At least 15 people were reported killed, with later reporting putting the toll at 17; homes, schools, a children’s hospital, warehouses and infrastructure were damaged. Ukraine reported high interception rates against drones and cruise missiles but identified ballistic missiles as its principal vulnerability.

**Why it matters:** The attack underscores mounting pressure on Ukraine’s air defences ahead of winter. President Volodymyr Zelensky said delayed replenishment of Patriot interceptors was costing lives and weakening Ukraine’s ability to protect cities and military production.

### 2. North Korea responds to reduced allied drills with missile barrage
North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area, each flying roughly 300 kilometres toward the sea. The launch followed Washington’s decision to shorten the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea and President Donald Trump’s statement that he expected to meet Kim Jong Un this year.

**Why it matters:** Pyongyang has shown that a limited reduction in exercises is insufficient to restart diplomacy. Kim Yo Jong dismissed the measure while preserving the possibility of future talks by describing relations between Trump and Kim as “excellent.” The exercise reduction has also raised concerns about allied readiness.

### 3. Washington shifts toward intensified economic pressure on Iran
The Trump administration announced an “economic D-Day” campaign against Iran, threatening secondary sanctions against countries, companies and financial institutions maintaining ties with Tehran. The move follows the expiration of a 60-day diplomatic memorandum without a breakthrough and comes amid continued pressure around the Strait of Hormuz. Iran rejected the threats.

**Why it matters:** A stronger secondary-sanctions campaign could affect major Iranian trading partners, including China and India, as well as US allies. With no agreed diplomatic framework, incidents involving shipping, US forces or Iran-aligned groups could trigger renewed military escalation.

### 4. Israeli force posture shifts north amid tensions over Syria
Israel permanently relocated an Apache attack-helicopter squadron from Ramon Airbase to Ramat David in northern Israel. The move followed an Israeli strike on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase, which Israel said was intended to prevent a Turkish military deployment; Turkey and Syria disputed Israel’s account.

**Why it matters:** The relocation improves Israel’s response capacity toward Lebanon, Syria and the Golan Heights. The Syrian strike also highlights growing Israeli-Turkish competition over Syria’s future security order.

## WATCH

- **Ukraine’s air-defence supply:** Whether partners provide additional Patriot interceptors and anti-ballistic capabilities before further Russian attacks and the winter period.
- **Korean Peninsula diplomacy:** Any preparations for a Trump-Kim meeting, further North Korean launches, or additional changes to US-South Korean exercises.
- **Iran and the Strait of Hormuz:** Implementation of new US secondary sanctions, Iranian pressure on shipping, and any incident capable of restarting larger-scale fighting.

## U.S.–South Korea Drills Cut Short

The United States and South Korea ended the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises six days earlier than planned and cancelled some field training after President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction. Trump described the move as a conciliatory gesture toward North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Seoul reportedly received little advance notice, although the Pentagon said training objectives were not degraded.

**Why it matters:** The decision represents a significant shift in alliance signaling toward Pyongyang. It could create an opening for diplomacy, but the limited coordination and reduced training have also raised concerns about alliance management and readiness against a North Korean attack.

## North Korea Answers Overture With Missile Barrage

North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward its eastern waters. The missiles flew roughly 300 kilometers and may have been KN-25 systems, which Pyongyang says can carry tactical nuclear warheads. Kim Yo Jong dismissed the reduced exercises as insufficient while leaving open the possibility of future engagement by describing relations between Kim and Trump as “excellent.”

**Why it matters:** The launches demonstrate that Pyongyang is seeking larger concessions before resuming talks and continues to expand its missile capabilities. South Korean officials also cited outside estimates that North Korea may possess 80–120 nuclear warheads, underscoring the growing scale of the security challenge.

## China’s AI Sector Faces Advanced-Chip Constraints

Chinese AI companies are optimizing software and domestic processors to handle rapidly growing inference demand, but industry figures said complex, commercially valuable tasks such as coding still depend heavily on scarce Nvidia chips. China’s average daily AI token calls reportedly rose more than 1,000-fold from early 2024 to March.

**Why it matters:** Continued reliance on restricted foreign processors exposes a major vulnerability in China’s AI ambitions. Compute shortages could slow large-scale deployment, weaken commercialization and intensify Beijing’s efforts to develop competitive domestic semiconductors.

## WATCH

- **Prospects for Trump–Kim talks:** Monitor whether a proposed meeting later this year advances and what further concessions Pyongyang demands.
- **North Korean drone capabilities:** U.S. and South Korean forces are increasing counter-drone training amid reports that North Korea is developing Iranian- and Russian-derived attack drones.

## 1. Russia launches major combined strike on Kyiv

Russia attacked Kyiv and the surrounding region on 20 August with 168 drones and dozens of cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The latest reporting put the death toll at 17, with more than 40 injured. Residential buildings, a school, kindergarten, children’s hospital, warehouses and infrastructure were damaged. Russia said it targeted military-industrial and logistics facilities.

**Why it matters:** The attack demonstrates Russia’s continued capacity for large, complex barrages. Ukraine reported high interception rates against drones and cruise missiles but remained vulnerable to ballistic weapons. President Volodymyr Zelensky renewed calls for Patriot interceptors, saying Ukraine was prepared to purchase them and that shortages were costing lives.

## 2. Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major Russian refinery

Ukrainian drones reportedly targeted Lukoil’s Perm refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, causing a fire and temporary aviation restrictions. Ukraine had not commented on the reported operation. Russia said it intercepted 325 drones across numerous regions, although that figure was not independently verified. The attack followed reported strikes on several other Russian refineries.

**Why it matters:** Ukraine is sustaining a long-range campaign against Russia’s fuel-processing capacity, potentially affecting domestic supplies, military logistics and export earnings. The geographic reach of the reported Perm strike also indicates continued expansion of Ukraine’s deep-strike capability.

## 3. Ukraine sets new defence priorities under Khmara

Ukraine’s parliament appointed Yevhenii Khmara as defence minister. Zelensky directed him to audit agreements with foreign partners, prioritize air and ballistic-missile defence, accelerate domestic missile programmes and increase deep-strike operations. Mobilization, troop rotations, military contracts and rising war costs were also identified as urgent issues.

**Why it matters:** The appointment signals an effort to align procurement, force management and long-range strike operations as Ukraine prepares for winter. Implementation will affect Ukraine’s ability to protect critical infrastructure, sustain manpower and finance an increasingly expensive war.

## WATCH

- **Patriot availability and winter attacks:** Monitor whether the United States and European partners provide additional interceptors, and whether Russia intensifies strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
- **Russian refinery disruption:** Assess confirmed damage and production losses from Ukrainian drone attacks, as well as any Russian military or economic response.

## 1. US shifts Iran campaign toward intensified economic pressure

**What happened:** President Donald Trump announced an expanded campaign of economic isolation against Iran after a 60-day negotiating framework expired without a diplomatic breakthrough. US officials threatened secondary sanctions against countries and companies trading with Iran, while the Navy continues its blockade around Iranian ports and the Strait of Hormuz. The USS George Washington has arrived to relieve the long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln, maintaining a substantial US naval presence.

**Why it matters:** The shift may reduce the likelihood of an immediate major military escalation, but it does not end the conflict. Aggressive sanctions and enforcement could affect Iranian oil buyers, particularly China and India, disrupt energy markets and increase the risk of confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz.

## 2. Israeli strike sharpens tensions with Turkey in Syria

**What happened:** Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur air base, saying it sought to prevent a Turkish military presence that could threaten Israeli security and restrict its freedom of action over Syria. Turkey denied plans for a military deployment at the base, condemned the attack but said it was not considering retaliation. Israel also permanently moved an Apache attack-helicopter squadron to Ramat David air base in the north.

**Why it matters:** The episode highlights growing Israeli-Turkish competition over post-Assad Syria. Further Israeli strikes against sites associated with Turkish support could undermine Syrian stabilization and create escalation risks between two major regional military powers.

## 3. Iraqi faction hands long-range weapons to the state

**What happened:** An unidentified Iraqi armed faction reportedly transferred about 20 Iranian-made one-way attack drones and missiles to the Iraqi government in the presence of US representatives. The step forms part of Baghdad’s effort to establish a state monopoly over weapons and avert threatened US economic and financial sanctions. Several powerful Iran-aligned factions continue to reject disarmament.

**Why it matters:** The handover represents limited progress in reducing autonomous militia arsenals capable of cross-border attacks. However, resistance from leading Iran-aligned groups leaves Baghdad vulnerable to internal confrontation, renewed attacks on US or regional targets, and external sanctions.

## WATCH

- **Iran escalation risks:** Monitor shipping incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, enforcement of secondary sanctions and any Iranian missile or proxy attacks that could prompt renewed US strikes.
- **Regional security realignment:** Watch implementation of the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani Mecca defence agreement and reports that Washington may consider direct talks with Hezbollah to help end the Lebanon conflict.

### U.S. Army explores continued HAWK missile support

The U.S. Army issued a market-research notice seeking contractors capable of providing logistics, engineering, maintenance and testing support for HAWK air-defence systems operated by foreign partners, including Ukraine. The potential work would also include integration support involving Sentinel, NASAMS and short-range air-defence systems. The notice does not commit the Army to awarding a contract.

**Why it matters:** Sustaining the retired U.S. system could help partner countries maintain scarce air-defence capacity, particularly Ukraine. It also indicates continued U.S. reliance on older weapons inventories to support allies while newer systems remain in high demand.

### Data-center expansion becomes a U.S. electoral liability

President Donald Trump continues to promote AI data centers as sources of investment, employment and strategic advantage over China. However, candidates from both parties are distancing themselves from projects amid concerns about electricity prices, water use, pollution, noise and tax incentives. Republican campaign officials have warned that the issue could affect competitive races.

**Why it matters:** The backlash could slow infrastructure needed for U.S. AI development and complicate Washington’s effort to compete technologically with China. It also exposes tension between national economic-security objectives and local concerns over costs and environmental impacts.

### Democratic Socialists expand influence within Democratic politics

The Democratic Socialists of America reported membership above 120,000 and a series of primary and municipal-level gains by members or aligned candidates. The movement is seeking a larger congressional presence and greater influence over Democratic positions on economic, immigration and foreign-policy issues.

**Why it matters:** Continued electoral gains could shift Democratic policy and candidate selection to the left ahead of the midterms. The movement’s ability to reproduce victories beyond strongly progressive constituencies will determine its broader national impact.

### WATCH

- Whether the Army proceeds from preliminary market research to a HAWK sustainment contract, especially one supporting Ukraine.
- State or federal measures addressing data centers’ electricity and water costs as electoral pressure increases.

articles.title: Osan Drills Target North Korea’s Growing Drone Threat
articles.body:
Some 50 miles from the border with North Korea, U.S. and South Korean forces recently executed their first counter-drone defense drills targeting medium-sized systems, which the North Korean military has has prioritized based on Russia and Iranian models.
Airmen, Soldiers, and Marines conducted exercise Dragon Flight from Aug. 2-6 at Osan Air Base, according to a 51st Fighter Wing release. The drills were conducted before President Donald Trump scaled back the recent larger, peninsula-wide, annual Ulchi Freedom Shield.
The exercise helped service members practice defending the F-16C/D fighters at Osan, which in turn defend against threats such as North Korea. The base’s primary mission is to launch waves of fighter jets in a potential conflict.
“This exercise helped all the involved agencies assess and validate their respective C-UAS defense systems,” 1st Lt. Thu Le with the 51st Security Forces Squadron said in the release. “I hope that this event gives the 51st Fighter Wing confidence in its current air defense capabilities and just shows how crucial such systems are to the defense of the base, its assets, and all 16,000 joint-force personnel.”
The exercise gave Osan a chance to train on a portion of air defense it hasn’t always focused on: Group 3 drones. These systems fall between smaller Group 1 and 2 threats and larger, legacy ballistic missiles, both of which personnel at Osan and Kunsan Air Bases have trained to defeat.
Alongside the service members conducting the counter-drone training were contractors from Griffin Aerospace, which operated the Outlaw Drone to simulate hostile aircraft.
Members of the 51st Security Forces Squadron used the Expeditionary Mobile Air Defense System to beat back the threat.
Soldiers with the 35th Air Defense Brigade used the AN/TWQ Avenger system while Marines with the 2nd Low Altitude Air Defense Battalion used Stinger man-portable missiles with Smart Shooter SMASH optics, according to the release.
Republic of Korea personnel also worked in the exercise with their own equipment.
The Bigger Picture
This training comes as U.S. bases and forward-deployed units face an ever-increasing drone threat, especially from Group 3 drones, which weigh between 50 and 1,320 pounds, fly up to 18,000 feet at speeds under 250 knots, and cost between $20,000 and $50,000 to produce.
During Operation Epic Fury, Iran has launched an estimated 2,000 Shahed-136 drones, which are Group 3, at U.S. and allied forces in the region, forcing the U.S. to use expensive munitions to take them down.
An Iranian one-way drone hit a U.S. facility in the Port of Shuaiba, Kuwait, on June 1, killing six U.S. soldiers.
Russia has used Iranian technology to build its own one-way attack drones, and North Korea has contributed troops and weapons to Russia in its war against Ukraine. In turn, Russia has reportedly helped North Korea to copy the Shahed and begin building factory lines to produce the knockoffs in 2025. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called drone production an “essential requirement” and a “top priority and important task” for modernizing the nation’s military.
Prior to the Shahed focus, North Korea used its own drones to conduct perimeter incursions into the Demilitarized Zone between North and South Korea in December 2022.
Since then, local news reports say smaller reconnaissance drones have been spotted in South Korean border cities from 2024 to 2025.
While both Osan and Kunsan Air Bases in South Korea have MIM-104 Patriot Systems for ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and fighter jets, as well as short-range air defense systems such as the AN/TWQ Avenger system, those are mainly geared toward low-altitude aircraft, cruise missiles, and helicopters.
Kunsan has not yet conducted a specific counter-drone exercise for Group 3 drones. However, Kunsan personnel have conducted exercises such as Beverley Sentinel, using red teams to test defenses against Group 1 and 2 drones.

articles.title: Mecca Defence Pact marks the start of a post-American Arab Gulf
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Mecca Defence Pact marks the start of a post-American Arab Gulf
Saudi figures put the number of Iranian missiles and drones fired towards the kingdom by late March at more than 700. Washington had launched the war alongside Israel a month earlier, yet Saudi air defences did most of the intercepting, and Riyadh spent the following months protecting its cities and oil infrastructure.
The American security guarantee in the Gulf broke when Saudi air defences took over, not when the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on 7 August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. The deal is often cited as evidence that the US-led order has ended, but in reality, it is paperwork that arrived four months late.
The retrenchment it supposedly announces has been underway since 2008. The financial crisis, the exhaustion of Iraq and Afghanistan and the turn towards competition with China pushed Washington away from occupation and towards sanctions, airpower and financial coercion. It is a model of regime management that imposes outcomes on other states while avoiding the cost of holding their territory.
The second pillar is burden-shifting, pressing partners to absorb the frontline costs of American strategy while Washington keeps the escalation umbrella. The Abraham Accords were its most over-engineered expression, trying to lock in regional enforcement through Israel that most Gulf states refused to join.
Set against that strategy, three states arming themselves while keeping their American relationships intact is not a rupture but a result. Turkey remains in NATO and continues to press for F-35s. Pakistan has spent this war as Washington’s channel to Tehran. And nine days before the ceremony in Mecca, Saudi Arabia flew joint strikes with US Central Command against Iran-aligned militias in Iraq.
A pact whose members are simultaneously fighting beside American forces, brokering for American diplomacy and shopping for American aircraft is not the end of an order; it is that order economising. In reality, it adds little to what the war had already shown. What matters is how it is being read in Tehran, and by whom.
The reading from Iran’s ruling bloc
The memorandum of understanding that preceded this summer’s fighting was engineered by Iran’s actual ruling class. This is the bloc organised around the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), the wider security establishment, the revolutionary-religious foundations (bonyads) that control much of the economy, and the Office of the Supreme Leader, which appoints their leadership and shields them from oversight.
Indeed, the bloc is not monolithic: a technocratic-economic wing holds that the Islamic Republic survives through economic recovery rather than ideological performance, while an ideological-maximalist wing, centred on the Paydari Front, regards engagement with Washington as futile.
The technocratic wing is in command, and its authority rests on institutions rather than personalities. When the truce collapsed on 8 July, it pushed Iran back into war rather than abandoning diplomacy, on the calculation that without control of Hormuz, Iran has nothing to sell when it returns to the table.
Its response to Mecca has been to shrink it. The IRGC-linked press warned negotiators against conceding anything, fearing a coalition that has not yet formed, because “the first defeat can occur not in war, but in the mind”. Other media outlets with similar political affiliations cited technical grounds: no joint command, no common fund, no automatic trigger.
The maximalists dissented, blaming President Masoud Pezeshkian for diplomacy too absorbed in Washington to see the pact coming, but they are weaker than their volume suggests.
More telling is what the security establishment was doing in the same days. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointed six senior commanders, installing Ahmad Vahidi as commander of the Revolutionary Guards and tasking the new chief of the Armed Forces General Staff with folding that body into the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, Iran’s wartime joint command. Days later, Mohsen Rezaei, who had run the Guards for 16 years, took over the Supreme National Security Council.
Some read this as the leadership clipping the technocratic wing; it overreads a single appointment, since Rezaei comes from the same establishment and the week’s direction was consolidation rather than redistribution.
The reshuffle shows a certain disposition. A bloc that folds its general staff into a wartime command does not see a defence pact among neighbours as its main problem. It has already adjusted to a region where Washington no longer guarantees outcomes. Its strategy was built for this reality.
A danger that needs no clause
On the narrow question, the bloc is likely correct. The collective defence article will not bring Turkish or Pakistani soldiers into a war with Iran. But the pact does not need to operate militarily to harm Iran. Here, composure becomes a risk.
The first exposure is political, and it builds over time. Iran’s neighbours are forming regional arrangements without it. Erdogan has said that Egypt could join. Each new member makes the next step easier and less costly to dismiss Iranian objections.
The second is economic, and no longer hypothetical. Twenty years of sanctions have produced an economy whose lifelines run overland and through re-export hubs, and the three that matter are Turkey, Pakistan and, above all, the United Arab Emirates.
On 18 August, after two Iranian ballistic missiles were fired towards its territory, Abu Dhabi suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice. In one announcement, Iran lost its largest commercial partner in the Gulf and the principal channel through which the bloc has moved goods and money around sanctions for two decades.
This is the real risk. The pact is more dangerous than its text implies. The two overland routes Iran still has are controlled by states now tied to Riyadh by mutual defence obligations. They do not need to use force. Slower customs, tighter banking, or a closed border would do more harm than any defence clause. Iran cannot respond to a NATO member and a nuclear-armed neighbour as it does to American bases in the Gulf.
This is where the ruling bloc’s strategy is most exposed. Its wager is that Iran returns to negotiations holding Hormuz and converts that leverage into investment and sanctions relief. Ghalibaf has reiterated that the strait will remain closed until Washington lifts its blockade and releases Iran’s frozen assets. But Trump now says there are no talks under way, and everything meant to follow a deal requires neighbours willing to trade with Iran.
For now, downplaying the Mecca pact serves its purpose. It steadies Iran’s negotiators and protects the economic programme that underpins the bloc’s authority. But this is composure, not analysis. A bloc organised for war can judge military threats but is less able to see dangers that do not take military form. Iran is not being encircled. It is being excluded from the arrangements its neighbours are making, and its own actions are speeding up that process. If this continues, the reckoning will come not on the battlefield but in the accounts.
Kayhan Valadbaygi is a Research Fellow at the International Institute of Social History (IISH) in Amsterdam and CEO of Middle East Risk & Reform Advisory.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill 17 in Ukraine, Zelensky says lack of Patriots costing lives
articles.body:
Russian strikes kill 17 in Ukraine, Zelensky says lack of Patriots costing lives
- Russian airstrikes on Aug 20 killed 17 people and damaged homes, schools, and hospitals in Kyiv and nearby areas, with Zelensky calling it a large-scale, cynical attack.
- Zelensky criticised allies for not replenishing Ukraine's Patriot missile stock, saying it costs lives and weakens defence against ballistic missile attacks.
- Strikes also hit food warehouses and infrastructure, causing supply issues and power outages; drones fell in Romania and Moldova amid ongoing military actions and stalled peace talks.
AI generated
KYIV - Russian air strikes killed 17 people and injured more than 40 in Kyiv and the surrounding region on Aug 20 as President Volodymyr Zelensky said a failure by Ukraine’s allies to replenish its stock of air defence missiles was costing lives.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched dozens of cruise missiles, as well as ballistic and hypersonic ones, and 168 drones, in a massive overnight attack.
The air force said that nearly 90 per cent of the drones and most of the cruise missiles were downed. It did not specify whether any of the more deadly ballistic missiles were intercepted – having said last week that providing such information was giving Russia cause to celebrate.
Zelensky called the Aug 20 strike one of the most “cynical, calculated, and large-scale” of the 4½ year war.
The upper floors of a nine-storey residential block were destroyed in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district, where at least eight people were killed, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. He declared Aug 21 a day of mourning.
World’s response ‘not adequate’, says Zelensky
Outside the damaged apartment block, an elderly woman wailed as rescuers carried out the body of her grandson.
She stood sobbing beside his body after he was placed on the ground, before medics came to support her.
Overall, 30 residential buildings, a school, a children’s hospital and a kindergarten were among those damaged in Kyiv and the surrounding areas, Zelensky said.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said that Moscow had used airstrikes and drones to hit targets in and around Kyiv, including facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub.
As Russia has escalated its ballistic strikes in recent months, Zelensky has pleaded with allies to replenish Ukraine’s stock of Patriot interceptors – the only weapon in its arsenal capable of downing a ballistic missile.
“Each additional missile saves the lives of our people,” Zelensky said on the Telegram app, adding that replacement missiles had not been received.
“Unfortunately... the world’s response to such attacks is not always adequate.”
Food warehouses damaged
Zelensky warned that Moscow would not seriously negotiate for peace as long as Ukraine had no missile defences to defend its cities. US-mediated talks to end the war stalled earlier this year as Kyiv refused to yield to Russian demands to cede more territory.
EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on X, in response to Zelensky’s message, that she was working with member states and partners to provide Ukraine with anti-ballistic capabilities as “the most urgent of priorities”.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said that some food warehouses and the facilities of the Red Cross around Kyiv were damaged in the overnight attack, which lasted nearly nine hours.
In recent weeks, fresh fruit and vegetables have occasionally disappeared from the shelves in some supermarkets in Kyiv as a result of strikes on logistics depots of food retailers.
Drones come down in Romania and Moldova
Sporadic attacks continued into the evening on Aug 20. For the first time in months, Russia targeted critical infrastructure in the capital, Klitschko said.
As a result, residents in two districts of Kyiv could see their hot water disrupted, he said - a grim reminder of winter bombardments that left many residents without heat and power for days at a time.
While most of the dead were in the Ukrainian capital, one person was also killed in the surrounding region, an official said on Telegram.
The Russian strikes also targeted a border crossing with Moldova in the Black Sea region of Odesa, where repeated attacks on ports and ships have brought Ukraine’s vital agricultural exports to a virtual halt, pressuring global food prices.
Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow’s ability to wage war.
Ukraine’s military said on Aug 20 it struck the TANECO oil refinery in Tatarstan and an oil terminal in Krasnodar region.
A drone crashed into Romania, a NATO and European Union member state, during the Russian attack on Ukraine, the Romanian defence ministry said. Another drone came down on Moldovan territory, President Maia Sandu said.
Ukraine has handed peace proposals to US negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, for a plan to end the war, Zelensky said in August.
The Kremlin said on Aug 20 there was no information yet on a possible visit to Moscow by Kushner and Witkoff, who were last in the Russian capital in January and have not yet visited Kyiv.
No date has yet been confirmed for a proposed visit to Ukraine, according to one source familiar with the discussions. REUTERS

articles.title: The US-Iran war is entering a dangerous new phase
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The US-Iran war is entering a dangerous new phase
Signed on 17 June, the vaguely worded Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), frequently referred to as a “memorandum of misunderstanding”, expired on 17 August.
Although the Islamabad MoU was intended to give Washington and Tehran 60 days for talks, the two sides have failed to achieve a diplomatic breakthrough.
At this point, the US-Iran confrontation is entering a new period which will likely be shaped by continued sanctions, pressure around the Strait of Hormuz, threats, negotiations, and limited military activity.
A legitimate concern is that a minor incident involving shipping, US military forces, or Iran-backed non-state actors could trigger a return to all-out war even if neither the Trump administration nor the Islamic Republic would desire such a nightmarish scenario.
In this next phase of the US-Iran crisis, the Strait of Hormuz is set to remain at the heart of the confrontation. Preserving freedom of navigation and preventing Tehran from using the strategic waterway as a source of leverage are top priorities for Washington.
Nonetheless, Iran’s effective control of the Strait of Hormuz is central to the Islamic Republic’s strategies for pressuring the United States into making concessions to Tehran.
In an effort to force Iran into accepting the Trump administration’s conditions for ending this crisis, Washington’s strategy rests on a combination of informational, economic, and military instruments, explained Wolfgang Pusztai, a senior advisor at the Austrian Institute for European and Security Policy.
“I would like to emphasise that the sharpest sword in the US strategy is not strikes, but economic instruments such as sanctions and the naval blockade. As long as Iran does not attack commercial ships and other targets in the region, there is no urgent need for the US to strike Iran,” he told The New Arab.
Trump appears intent on waiting until the sanctions and blockade take effect. However, as we have seen, the US will almost certainly resume strikes if Iran renews attacks on shipping in the Strait or on Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members, noted Pusztai.
If the US has reliable intelligence on the location of Iran’s remaining ballistic missiles and transporter erector launchers, a targeted one- to two-week campaign could significantly reduce the threat to GCC states and US bases in the region, he added.
“What we will likely see is a continuation of the sanctions and of the naval blockade with limited strikes in response to eventual larger military provocations by Iran. For Trump, a continued low-level war outside of the US media spotlight is certainly better than a humiliating defeat, especially before the midterm elections,” the Austrian defence and security analyst explained to The New Arab.
“On the other hand, Iran might try to draw the US again into a larger, more costly military confrontation to further undermine American domestic acceptance of the war further on,” he added.
Since the Islamabad MoU began unravelling, there has been a pattern of limited military exchanges, escalating threats, coercive diplomacy, and increased pressure on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, noted Dr Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House. He expects continuation of this pattern following the MoU’s expiration.
Yet, Dr Quilliam stressed that both the US and Iran maintain strong incentives to prevent this crisis from becoming a prolonged conflict.
“The Trump administration remains under pressure to demonstrate that its military campaign achieved tangible results, while Iran is seeking to preserve regime stability and avoid further damage to its economy and infrastructure,” he told The New Arab.
Nonetheless, given that the two sides are operating without any agreed framework since 17 August, there is a real risk that any “serious incident in the Gulf, an attack on US assets, or a confrontation involving shipping could rapidly trigger a renewed cycle of military action,” as Dr Quilliam noted, assessing that “full-scale operations therefore cannot be ruled out, but they are more likely to result from escalation and misjudgement than from a deliberate decision by either side to return to war”.
There is good reason to expect a continuation of the same cycle that has been repeated this year amid the US-Iran confrontation since April, entailing escalating threats, negotiations, and overly optimistic claims from Trump or his coterie that an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is imminent, explained Gordon Gray, the former US ambassador to Tunisia.
“The cycle repeats like clockwork once the promised agreement fails to materialise,” observed the former American diplomat.
“The senior-most ranks of the US military have already advised Trump that…the United States has reached the point of diminishing returns in terms of the effectiveness of strikes against Iran and…the United States is rapidly depleting its stocks of military materiel,” Gray told The New Arab.
“This reality, coming on top of the deep and growing unpopularity of the war, suggests that Trump would ultimately refrain from full-scale military operations against Iran.”
Iran's 'wait out Trump' strategy
The leadership in Tehran sees time on Iran’s side. This assumes that mounting economic pressure, rising fuel prices, and opposition to the war ahead of the US midterm elections will eventually force Washington to make concessions in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
This might prove to be a winning strategy for Iran. But Tehran is undeniably accepting serious risks and perhaps overestimating the importance of the US’s electoral calendar.
Dr Quilliam believes that Iran is “misguided” in taking for granted that the resolve in Washington will fade before Iran loses its ability to weather the economic and military costs of this confrontation.
“The longer the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz continues, the greater the strain on Iran's economy and the higher the risk of further military action against Iranian assets,” he told The New Arab.
“Tehran may calculate that time is on its side, but delaying meaningful engagement could allow the US to tighten pressure, build broader international support, and justify additional measures. In that sense, Iran is not pursuing a low-risk waiting game. It is gambling that it can withstand a prolonged confrontation better than its adversary.”
Gray’s view is that Tehran is failing to recognise differences between Trump’s political calculations today and those of President Jimmy Carter in 1980.
Whereas Carter was seeking re-election throughout most of the 1979-81 hostage crisis, Trump is not running for another term. “[Trump] apparently believes, and may well be correct, that the Republican Party will maintain control of the Senate. In short, he is not as concerned about the midterm elections as the Iranian leadership thinks or hopes,” said Gray.
The scale of Iran’s economic problems and the widespread suffering across the country is enormous, and how long the Islamic Republic can last under such dire conditions is an open question.
Given these extreme dynamics inside Iran, Dr Nader Hashemi, director of Georgetown University's Prince Alwaleed bin Talal Center for Muslim-Christian Understanding, believes that Iran’s strategy is perhaps a case of Tehran overplaying its hand.
“By not pursuing negotiations and saying it’s going to wait out the Trump administration before it considers diplomacy with the United States, that effectively means that Iran will not get meaningful sanctions relief or economic relief for the next two and a half years. The Iranian economy and the plight of the average citizen in Iran is catastrophic,” he told The New Arab.
“The level of pain, suffering, unemployment, rising inflation, and inability of people to meet their basic life needs - and I’m talking about purchasing food - has risen to new catastrophic levels, and this has been exacerbated by the American blockade on Iran,” added Dr Hashemi.
An expanding conflict
There is a real danger that the US-Iran crisis will extend beyond the current confrontation between Washington and Tehran, with the expiration of the Islamabad MoU making containment of this conflict increasingly challenging.
The risk of more regional states being increasingly pulled into this crisis, either directly or indirectly, is real.
Particularly alarming is the military threat that Trump issued against Oman at the time of the Islamabad MoU’s expiration. As a longstanding intermediary between the United States and Iran, Muscat has played an important role in keeping diplomatic channels open.
Even if the US taking military action against the country is an extremely unlikely scenario, Trump’s threats to do so nonetheless risk damaging Washington’s relationship with Muscat at a time in which a strong US-Oman partnership is key to de-escalation.
“President Trump’s threat of attacking Oman is a continuation of his diplomacy by threats,” said Dr Shireen Hunter, an honorary fellow at the Center for Muslim-Christian Understanding at Georgetown University who served as an Iranian diplomat before 1979, in an interview with The New Arab.
“With increasing opposition to the war with Iran in Congress, extending the war to Oman would be very unwise. Moreover, such an attack would further undermine US standing with Persian Gulf Arab states. In addition, attacking Oman would not change Tehran's mind regarding an agreement with the US,” she added.
This threat against Oman speaks to Trump’s “deeply authoritarian governing style” in which he believes he can “coerce other countries to follow his policies,” Dr Hashemi told The New Arab.
He also explained that “it makes no practical sense that the United States would start bombing its own allies in the Middle East and the fact that Donald Trump is actually making these types of threats highlights the total incoherence of US foreign policy”.
As Gray sees it, Trump’s second threat to bomb Oman was “bizarre” and reflective of the president’s “frustration and impetuosity as well as the fact that he has no idea whatsoever how to extricate the United States from the war he started with Iran”.
Yemen is another flashpoint that can’t be ignored when considering the potential expansion of the US-Iran crisis now that the Islamabad MoU has expired.
Given the Houthis’ ability to threaten commercial shipping and maritime infrastructure in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, it is necessary to consider how an uptick in Ansar Allah’s attacks could force Washington to respond militarily, potentially creating a second major front at a time when Washington is already attempting to manage the confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz.
The result could be a widening cycle in which Iranian pressure through regional partners generates additional US military action, which in turn prompts further retaliation.
“Developments in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden may prove just as important as events in the Strait of Hormuz in shaping the next phase of the crisis,” Dr Quilliam told The New Arab.
A far more extreme possibility is the prospect of the conflict entering an entirely new and far more dangerous phase, as noted by Dr Hunter, who pointed to reports that the United States may be considering the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Iran, while stressing that this possibility remains contingent on whether those claims are accurate.
Even without such an escalation, the combination of Iran-backed non-state actors, attacks on shipping, US military responses and threats against regional states creates significant potential for miscalculation.
Therefore, a central concern is not simply whether Washington or Tehran deliberately chooses a wider war, but whether a series of escalating actions and reactions gradually leads to such an outcome.
In that sense, the Islamabad MoU’s expiration matters not only because it removes a diplomatic framework, but because it may leave fewer mechanisms for preventing a localised crisis from further regionalising and internationalising.
Can diplomacy prevent escalation?
In this confrontation, neither Washington nor Tehran appears willing to make the first significant concession. Although under mounting economic and military pressure, Iran’s leadership lacks any incentive to accept an agreement that could be seen by a domestic audience as surrender to the United States and Israel.
Meanwhile, Washington has climbed a tall tree that would be humiliating for it to climb down given how much the Trump administration has invested in trying to demonstrate that military and economic pressure can force Tehran to change course.
However, Washington is not in a position to ignore the costs of a prolonged conflict, including declining domestic support, military constraints, and the risk of a wider regional war.
Consequently, the US and Iran find themselves in a dangerous stalemate in which both sides seem to calculate that maintaining pressure will result in the other eventually blinking despite the fact that neither Washington nor Tehran can be entirely certain about how much pressure the other side can actually withstand.
Within this context, diplomacy is the most important and most underused instrument in the crisis. As Pusztai explained, Washington’s strategy has relied heavily on economic and military pressure while devoting insufficient attention to building political coalitions and creating diplomatic pathways out of the conflict.
The challenge now is to find a way for the US and Iran to step back in manners that allow both sides to save face. The most serious danger may therefore be less a deliberate decision by Washington or Tehran to launch a wider war than a series of miscalculations that gradually makes escalation unavoidable.
The Islamabad MoU’s expiration has narrowed the space for managing those risks, making the search for credible diplomatic off-ramps all the more urgent.

articles.title: North Korea launches missiles as Trump seeks to rekindle nuclear talks
articles.body:
North Korea launches ballistic missiles as Trump seeks to rekindle nuclear talks with Kim Jong Un
Seoul — North Korea fired several short-range ballistic missiles, Seoul's military said Thursday, hours after President Trump said he would meet again with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un later this year.
 The latest launches by the nuclear-armed North came after Mr. Trump ordered a reduction in the ongoing joint South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises, which are now set to end Friday.
 
Pyongyang has long condemned U.S.-South Korean exercises as rehearsals for an invasion, often staging missile test launches during and around the drills.
Mr. Trump said he made the decision to scale back the war games "based on my very good relationship with" Kim. He said the longstanding annual military exercises sent a "totally inappropriate and hostile signal" to the North.
South Korea's lack of assistance in the war with Iran was also a factor, he said.
The president said it was important to "get along" with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons.
Officials in Seoul said Thursday that North Korea now has between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads, and they couldn't explain the discrepancy between their estimate and Mr. Trump's.
Just hours after Mr. Trump said he expected to meet again with Kim, an official from Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff told the AFP that the North had fired "around 10 short-range ballistic missiles" from the Pyongyang area.
Japan earlier said a suspected "ballistic missile launched by North Korea a short while ago has already fallen," according to an X post from the prime minister's office.
Mr. Trump's sudden focus on Kim and his scaling back of the joint drills with South Korea have alarmed Asian allies, sparking speculation that he may be seeking a foreign policy win as the Iran war grinds on in a costly stalemate.
Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader's powerful sister, said Wednesday that her brother had "good memories and feelings" about Mr. Trump and that the relationship between the two leaders remained "excellent."
She said, however, that she was unaware of any current communication between the two leaders.
Mr. Trump met three times with Kim during his first term, lauding his relations with the authoritarian leader but failing to get him to make any solid commitments to rein in North Korea's nuclear weapons program, which has advanced steadily since.
Her statement came hours after Seoul announced the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises would end on Friday — about a week earlier than planned — "at the suggestion of the U.S. side."
The Pentagon said the reduced drills would cause "no degradation to U.S. training objectives."
The exercises are designed to prepare for a possible attack by North Korea.
The United States has about 28,500 forces stationed in South Korea to bolster the country's defenses — a legacy of the 1950-53 Korean War that ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
South Korea's Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back said Seoul remained opposed to officially recognizing the North as a nuclear-weapon state, something Kim has long sought.
Asked whether Washington had "given up" on North Korea's denuclearization, Ahn said he did not believe so.
President Lee Jae Myung, who has long pushed for stronger homegrown defenses to reduce South Korea's reliance on the United States, said Wednesday that he would "do his utmost" to support Mr. Trump's peacemaking efforts with the North.

articles.title: US, South Korean militaries wrapping up drills early, a day after North Korea’s missile barrage
articles.body:
US, South Korean militaries wrapping up drills early, a day after North Korea’s missile barrage
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — The U.S. and South Korean militaries were wrapping up their annual drills six days earlier than initially scheduled on Friday in a conciliatory gesture toward North Korea, though the North said the step isn’t enough to convince it to return to talks.
U.S. President Donald Trump had earlier abruptly ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises just before they began Monday. Trump cited what he described as a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to support him over the war in Iran.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, brushed aside Trump’s overture on Wednesday, saying “the provocative, aggressive nature of the drills” won’t change only with the reduction of their duration and size.
The next day, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, apparently following through with its previous threat to respond to the U.S.-South Korean drills that it views as an invasion rehearsal.
The U.S. Pacific Command said the events didn’t pose an immediate threat to U.S. territory or its allies. The command said the U.S. remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and its allies in the region.
Kim Yo Jong’s statement dampened hopes for an early resumption of talks between Trump and Kim Jong Un, whose earlier nuclear diplomacy collapsed in 2019. Kim Jong Un has used the diplomatic stalemate to increase his leverage by modernizing his nuclear and missile programs and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine. Kim Jong Un suggested last year that he won’t return to talks unless the U.S. drops its demand for North Korean denuclearization as a precondition for diplomacy.
Kim Yo Jong still used relatively measured language, avoided typical harsh North Korean rhetoric and touched upon what she called an “excellent” relationship between her brother and Trump. This suggests North Korea doesn’t want to completely shut the door for future talks and may seek to win bigger U.S. concessions, such as international recognition as a nuclear state and broad sanctions relief.
With its supply of ammunition and troops to Russia, North Korea is likely receiving economic and military assistance in return, and its expanding ties with Russia provides it with leverage to ask for greater support from China, its biggest trading partner.
“After this strategic play has run its course, Kim may seek further economic and reputational benefits from Washington,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. “But that will probably be after the U.S. midterm elections when Trump is expected to be in a weaker domestic political position and in search of headline-grabbing foreign policies.”
Kim Dong-yub, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said that Kim Yo Jong’s statement showed North Korea’s position that a personal relationship between her brother and Trump “can’t be a factor that moves current North Korean-U.S. relations.” He said Kim Yo Jong likely aimed to head off speculation that Trump’s move can restore diplomacy so as not to fully take the blame when it doesn’t happen.
Kim Yo Jong denied Trump’s claim that Kim Jong Un had responded to his request for a conversation. When asked by reporters Wednesday if he would be meeting with Kim Jong Un this year, Trump said that “Yeah, I will be.”
The Ulchi Freedom Shield is one of the main military exercises conducted by the U.S. and South Korea annually to enhance their ability to cope with potential North Korean aggression. Its downsizing has caused worries about joint U.S.-South Korean readiness.

Nuclear Secrets as Payment: How Russia May Have Funded Its Iranian Drones
Russia paid for Iranian Shahed attack drones using gold, hard currency, and UAE dirhams transferred to shell company accounts, according to Molfar Intelligence Institute on August 20.
However, two names in the payroll records of the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, Russia, suggest that nuclear know-how may have served as an additional form of payment.

On March 10, 2023, two individuals whose background is unrelated to aviation traveled on a flight from Russia to Iran. The first individual is Russian engineer Dmitry Shubnyakov.
Formally listed as a digital electronics software engineer at the Alabuga facility—specifically in the unit producing "motorboats," the Russian internal codename for domestically manufactured Shahed drones—Shubnyakov spent his entire career working on nuclear infrastructure.
His expertise focused on spent nuclear fuel management, weapons-grade plutonium facilities, and specialized servicing robotics.
Ten days before his flight to Tehran, his name appeared as an inventor on an international patent application for robotic repair systems used in spent nuclear fuel storage pools.
The second individual is Iranian researcher Saeid Darkhi, who lives in Yekaterinburg and conducts research at Ural Federal University. His work centers on metal forming under pressure, a technology applied in the manufacturing of nuclear fuel storage containers.
In July 2025, a person with this name received an international patent. Although both men received payments from Alabuga for over two years, Shubnyakov was registered in a position that did not match his actual activity, while Darkhi was paid under a one-off service contract without being assigned to a specific department.
Analysts at the Molfar Intelligence Institute traced both individuals through Alabuga payroll records covering the 2023–2025 period, when Russia localized Shahed drone production. The investigation examined whether these payments were linked to technology transfers or royalties for inventions and research.
Shubnyakov previously worked at the Special Design and Technology Bureau of Applied Robotics, a Moscow-based contractor with historical ties to Chernobyl cleanup operations and clients including Rosatom and the Russian Ministry of Defense.
His patents address repair issues in spent fuel storage pools—a technical area historically relevant to plutonium production reactors and spent fuel management agreements between Russia and Iran.
Darkhi’s academic research focuses on seamless tube manufacturing and titanium alloys, which are used in nuclear energy and spent fuel storage. Citations of his work link him to researchers at Iranian institutions connected to Iran's nuclear and missile programs.
Western media previously documented visits by Iranian scientists to Russian nuclear research centers in 2024, where they inquired about tritium, strontium-90, nickel-63, and laser technology useful for nuclear testing simulation.
According to intelligence reports and leaked documents from the Iranian entity Sahara Thunder, initial payments for Shahed drones involved 2,000 kilograms of gold bullion delivered by spring 2023, along with cash transactions routed through Dubai-based entities.
Ukrainian intelligence and independent researchers from C4ADS noted that bilateral defense cooperation expanded into broader military technology transfers beyond the drone project.
Molfar analysts suggest that payments funneled through Alabuga’s production expenses could have functioned as royalties or research compensation, framing nuclear technical knowledge as a non-monetary payment method for military hardware.
In March 2026, Russia openly declared its support for Iran amid escalating confrontations involving the United States and Israel, signaling that Moscow did not consider itself a neutral actor in the Middle East crisis.
Russian Ambassador to the United Kingdom Andrei Kelin confirmed that Moscow was siding with Tehran, criticizing Western governments for placing full blame on Iran while ignoring initial strikes by the US and Israel.
Pointing to the deepening strategic partnership between the two nations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kelin called for an immediate end to hostilities and a return to political dialogue rather than military escalation.

articles.title: North Korea Dismisses Trump’s Recent Overtures to Kim Jong Un
articles.body:
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said there was no communication between the leaders of the United States and North Korea, according to a statement published by the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on August 19.
“As for the news from Washington that shortly ago, there was a communication between the leaders of the DPRK and the U.S., I am not aware of it at all, and perhaps it may be the only thing I do not know as regards the foreign policy of our supreme leadership,” Kim said. (DPRK is an acronym of North Korea’s official name, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.)
It was the first response of Pyongyang to U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim that Kim Jong Un responded to his overtures. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump has discussed setting up a meeting with Kim Jong Un on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which will be held in November in Shenzhen, China.
In the past few days, Trump has made friendly gestures to Kim Jong Un. He posted a photo of him and Kim taking a stroll during the Hanoi Summit in 2019 and a meme of Kim making a phone call, with text suggesting he was calling Trump. On August 17, Trump said on his Truth Social account that he had ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” the joint military exercises with South Korea, which began on the same day. The Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises were supposed to last until August 27 but, according to local media reports, they will end on August 21.
South Korea’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Ministries said on August 19 that Washington had not explained or given advance notice regarding Trump’s decision to scale down the joint military exercises. However, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung showed a positive attitude, saying that he will remain fully dedicated to serving as “a peacemaker” to facilitate and contribute to Trump’s peacemaking endeavors.
As North Korea has long deemed the South Korea-U.S. joint military exercises as an invasion rehearsal, some expected that Pyongyang would at least make a reciprocal gesture. However, Kim Yo Jong clearly downplayed Trump’s decision to scale back the ongoing joint military exercises between the U.S. and South Korea.
“As for the reduction of the U.S.-ROK joint military drill abruptly announced by the U.S. president a few days ago, we regard it as the one unworthy of comment and have no interest in it at all,” Kim said. (ROK is an acronym of South Korea’s official name, Republic of Korea.) “The reduction of the scale and duration of the drill does not mean the change of the nature of the military drill with a provocative and offensive feature.”
In a separate statement published by KCNA a day later, also attributed to Kim Yo Jong, she mocked South Korea’s “poor plight” over the cancellation. “The ROK cannot let out a single word of protest at the GIs leaving without any mutual coordination at the U.S. chief executive’s unilateral order,” Kim said. “This is the inevitable fate of the puppet army.” She also compared the South Korea-U.S. alliance to “the relation between master and servant.” However, Kim still refrained from indicating any positive response on Pyongyang’s part to the reduction of the exercises.
Also on August 20, North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the ocean off its east coast, according to the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The missiles, which flew around 300 km, were launched from the Pyongyang area around 5 p.m. KST. The South Korean National Security Council convened an emergency meeting and condemned the North’s missile launches.
Despite her explicit accusation that the United States was maintaining its hostile policy against North Korea, Kim Yo Jong confirmed again that the relationship between Trump and Kim Jong Un is “still excellent,” which is the only confirmation of Pyongyang that matches what Trump has said in the past days.
Following Kim Yo Jong’s statement, Trump said North Korea possesses “57 very powerful nuclear weapons” and emphasized that he gets along with Kim Jong Un well. With that, Trump also said that he expects to meet with the North Korean leader later this year.
However, Ahn Gyu-back, the defense minister of South Korea, told lawmakers at the South’s National Assembly on August 21 that North Korea may have around 80 to 120 nuclear weapons. Ahn said that he could not share Seoul’s estimate of the exact number of the North’s nuclear weapons.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi happened to be visiting Seoul amid the furor over a potential Trump-Kim summit. In the meeting with his counterpart, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, on August 19, Wang said China will play a constructive role for peace on the Korean Peninsula. Regarding China’s role in a potential summit between Trump and Kim, Wang declined to comment, saying it is a matter for the U.S. and North Korea.

articles.title: 14 killed as Russia unleashes massive overnight barrage on unprotected Kyiv, striking homes, hospital, school and railway infrastructure
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing 14 people and injuring more than 40, Ukrainian authorities said on 20 August.
The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles alongside hundreds of drones. Ukraine’s Air Force said the main direction of the attack was Kyiv Oblast, with strikes and debris recorded at multiple locations. Several explosions were heard in the capital around midnight on 20 August, according to Euromaidan Press reporters in the city.
Residential building hit in Kyiv
In Kyiv, strikes, damage, and fires were reported in the Sviatoshynskyi, Darnytskyi, and Solomianskyi districts.
In Solomianskyi district, the upper two floors of a nine-story residential building were destroyed, with a fire breaking out across the seventh through ninth floors.
People were trapped in two residential buildings and a school bomb shelter, prompting emergency crews to carry out rescue operations.
Thirteen people have now been confirmed killed in Kyiv, including a woman whose body was discovered by rescuers in Solomianskyi district, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a children's hospital and a school were also damaged in the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city would observe 21 August as a day of mourning, with entertainment events banned and flags lowered.
Fires and damage across Kyiv
Around 20 residential buildings in Kyiv were significantly damaged, along with a school, children's hospital, and kindergarten, Vyhivskyi said.
In Sviatoshynskyi district, Russian strikes hit an industrial site and sparked fires at warehouses covering 500 and 1,000 square meters. Another warehouse also caught fire.
In Darnytskyi district, a non-residential site was hit, causing fires across warehouses and vehicles covering about 1,000 square meters. Rescuers saved one person and handed them over to medics.
Other locations saw damage to residential buildings, a medical facility, cars, garages, and stores.
More than 600 rescuers and police officers have been involved in clearing the aftermath since overnight. Emergency crews are currently working at two sites in Kyiv and three more in Boryspil and Brovary districts.
Rescuers are using specialized equipment and robotic systems to clear the rubble and check whether anyone remains trapped.
Police have set up assistance centers at the attack sites to register reports of damaged or destroyed property. More than 200 reports have already been processed in Kyiv, while psychologists are assisting people who lost relatives or their homes.
Kyiv Oblast casualties
The attack also hit Kyiv Oblast. One man was killed in Brovary district and another was injured.
In Boryspil district, six people were injured, four of whom were hospitalized. The attack damaged 14 private homes, four warehouses, a gas station, an apartment building, and eight vehicles.
Vyhivskyi said fires also engulfed warehouses storing household goods in Kyiv Oblast. Firefighters are working to contain the blaze, with aviation also deployed.
Zelenskyy calls for stronger ballistic missile defenses
Zelenskyy said Russia’s growing investment in ballistic missiles requires a stronger international response and more air defense for Ukraine.
He said Ukraine is working daily on its FREYJA interceptor program, but stressed that Patriot interceptors remain irreplaceable and are needed every day to protect Ukrainian cities from Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“Every additional missile saves the lives of our people,” Zelenskyy said, thanking those working to provide Ukraine with additional air defense capabilities.
Hundreds of aerial targets launched
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 168 Shahed-type attack drones, Gerbera decoy drones, and other drones, along with 36 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kh-59 cruise missiles, eight Kalibr missiles, two Banderyl-type loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles including Oniks, Zircon, Iskander-M, and S-400 missiles.
As of 9:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 31 cruise missiles, all eight Kalibr missiles, both loitering munitions, and 145 drones, according to the Air Force.
The Air Force reported impacts at 28 locations and debris from intercepted targets at two others.
The attack continued into the late morning, with air raid sirens still active and several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic and hypersonic missiles overnight, damaging a children’s hospital, with people trapped in a shelter
Rail traffic disrupted
Russia's strikes also disrupted rail traffic around Kyiv after railway infrastructure was damaged. Several suburban and regional trains between Kyiv and Nizhyn were rerouted or canceled.
Strikes reported in other regions
Zelenskyy said the attack also caused damage in Odesa and Chernihiv oblasts.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian drones targeted a border crossing with Moldova, while strikes in Chernihiv Oblast damaged gas infrastructure.

South Korea has traditionally avoided publicly disclosing detailed estimates of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal and does not officially recognize Pyongyang as a nuclear-armed state, in keeping with its longstanding policy of pursuing denuclearization.
“We cannot develop nuclear weapons. Nor should we agree to the deployment of U.S. tactical nuclear weapons,” Ahn Gyu-baek said.
The comments come as Trump seeks to revive dialogue with Kim Jong Un after ordering a reduction in the scale of joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises, which he described as hostile toward North Korea.
On August 15, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called on North Korea to engage in talks aimed at ensuring peaceful coexistence and replacing the armistice agreement with a full-fledged “peace regime.”

North Korea fires barrage of missiles toward the sea after dismissing overture from Trump
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, a day after the North shrugged off a U.S. decision to scale back military drills with South Korea in an apparent bid to resume diplomacy.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff said the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles happened from North Korea’s capital region around 5 p.m. (0800 GMT) on Thursday. The military said the missiles flew about 300 kilometers (185 miles) each toward North Korea’s eastern waters.
The military said South Korea has bolstered its surveillance posture and was closely coordinating information on the launches with the U.S. and Japan. South Korea’s presidential national security council issued a statement urging North Korea to halt ballistic missile launches.
The Japanese prime minister’s office had earlier said that it detected a suspected missile launch.
U.S. President Donald Trump earlier ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, just before they began Monday. Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with Kim and South Korea’s refusal to support him over the war in Iran.
On Wednesday, the South Korean and U.S. militaries confirmed they shortened the 11-day drills by shortening their duration by about half and canceling some field training exercises. The reduction of the exercises raised worries about the allies’ joint defense posture.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed Trump’s overture later Wednesday, saying “the provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won’t change even though their duration and size were reduced.”
“If the U.S. calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as the one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer,” she said in a statement.
She denied Trump’s claim that Kim Jong Un had responded to his request for a conversation.
Kim Yo Jong still refrained from the typical North Korean reaction of fiery rhetoric and said personal relations between her brother and Trump are “still excellent.” That signals North Korea would want to wait for Trump to make bigger concessions before returning to talks.
When asked by reporters Wednesday if he would be meeting with Kim Jong Un this year, Trump said that “Yeah, I will be.” He wouldn’t answer a question about whether he is exchanging letters with Kim but said he gets along with him.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield is one of the main military exercises conducted by the U.S. and South Korea annually to enhance their ability to cope with potential North Korean aggression. Washington and Seoul say their drills are defensive in nature, but North Korea calls them an invasion rehearsal and often reacts with weapons tests.
Before this month’s drills started, North Korea accused the U.S. and South Korea of plotting more provocative exercises this summer and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.” Days before the drills’ start, North Korea fired two ballistic missiles into the sea in its first such launches since late June.
Trump’s earlier diplomacy with Kim Jong Un collapsed in 2019 due to disputes over how much sanctions relief North Korea should be given in return for dismantling its main nuclear complex, a limited denuclearization step. Kim has since shunned any talks with the U.S., pushed to modernize weapons arsenals and expanded cooperation with Russia.
Kim has said he won’t place his nuclear program back on the negotiating table. Experts say Kim has more leverage than when he first held talks with Trump in 2018 and 2019. They say Kim likely hopes to eventually win international recognition as a nuclear state and extensive sanctions relief in exchange for only limited steps toward denuclearization.
__
Associated Press writer Mari Yamaguchi in Tokyo contributed to this report.

articles.title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills near end
articles.body:
North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills near end
South Korea convened an emergency security meeting following the launches, as Trump seeks to sway Pyongyang.
South Korea has condemned North Korea’s launch of more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles, following military drills between Seoul and Washington that US President Donald Trump is seeking to curb.

The North Korean missiles flew around 300km (186 miles) toward the sea, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
South Korean Defence Minister Ahn Gyu-back told lawmakers that the short-range ballistic missiles are believed to be 600 mm multiple rocket launchers, adding that Seoul has tracked them because they could be potentially deployed near its border with the South.
Pyongyang has previously described the 600 mm system, known externally as the KN-25, as being able to deliver tactical nuclear warheads. Ahn said earlier in the day that North Korea possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads.
Trump reduces drills in bid to court Pyongyang
The launch came after North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, on Wednesday condemned the US-South Korea military drills.
Trump cut the drills short – they are now set to end Friday – and said he wanted to revive diplomacy with leader Kim Jong Un.
Hours after the launches, Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, described Trump’s decision as “an evident disaster brought by the unrealistic and anachronistic security outlook” pursued by Seoul, arguing the South had a “master-and-servant” relationship with the US.
Trump said on Monday he had received a response from Kim Jong Un after scaling back the military exercises. However, Kim’s sister on Wednesday said she was unaware of any recent communications between the two countries’ leaders, maintaining the “hostile policy” of the US towards North Korea had not changed.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Thursday said Moscow “can only welcome” the US decision to cut back its participation in military exercises with South Korea.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who visited Seoul this week, urged South Korea not to take sides between Beijing and Washington, saying the US should abandon its “hostile” policy toward North Korea to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
