MOSCOW – Russia conducted a rare missile exercise involving naval vessels and a land-based launcher near islands in its Far East that are also claimed by Japan, adding to recent friction between the two nations.
Missiles were launched from a nuclear-powered submarine, a guided-missile cruiser and the Bastion coastal defence system around the Southern Kuril islands, the Russian Pacific Fleet said on Aug 20, without providing the date of the exercise, according to the Interfax news agency.
The missiles were fired at targets more than 300km away and hit them, according to the report.
The Pacific Fleet didn’t provide a precise location for the exercise, but Russia deployed Bastion coastal defence batteries on Iturup Island, known in Japan as Etorofu, in 2016.
In response to the exercise, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters: “Russia’s military buildup on the four Northern Islands runs counter to Japan’s position and is unacceptable,” according to Kyodo News.
The southern Kuril islands are controlled by Russia after the Soviet Union seized them from Japan in the final days of World War II.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the territory last week when he travelled to Iturup, prompting a protest from Tokyo.
Putin’s visit and the missile test come as Japan has aligned with western nations in support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian invasion, including the imposition of sanctions on Moscow.
Tokyo has also supplied non-lethal support for Ukraine’s military, including body armour and transport vehicles.
During his visit to the Far East, Putin said that Japan had recently changed its attitude toward Russia without provocation.
He criticised sanctions and said Russia had been described as a major threat in Japanese defence documents.
The dispute over the islands has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal World War II peace treaty.
While Russia’s possession of the Kurils is “enshrined in international documents,” Moscow was still prepared to seek a solution through a peace treaty with Japan, Putin said last week.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe sought to reach an agreement with Putin under which two of the islands would be returned to Japan, but since then there’s been little prospect of renewed dialogue.
Unlike her immediate predecessors, current Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has yet to hold talks Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, prompting some speculation that she might try to restart negotiations over the disputed islands with Russia. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Russian drones hit border crossing with Moldova in overnight strike, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The announcement comes a day after a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed an explosive-laden maritime drone close to Europe's largest offshore gas project.
A border crossing with Moldova in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region was damaged by Russian drones overnight, the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine said in a statement on Friday morning.
Traffic through the Tabaky checkpoint has been suspended and diverted to other crossings, the border service said on Telegram.
Moldovan authorities in Chișinău have been informed, the statement added.
The announcement comes a day after a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed an explosive-laden maritime drone close to Europe's largest offshore gas project, hours after another drone entered the NATO member's airspace and crashed near the Ukrainian border.
Romania's President Nicuşor Dan blamed Russia for the latest incident and condemned what he called an escalation of "irresponsible incidents" by Moscow.
Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled and one destroyed the drone after authorities decided it posed a potential threat to the hundreds of people working at the site and to critical energy infrastructure.
Defence Minister Radu Miruță said the drone was carrying explosives and that Kyiv had confirmed it was not Ukrainian.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the incident as part of "an escalating campaign of threats" against the European Union.
"This is hybrid warfare," she said, accusing those responsible of seeking to unsettle European citizens and divide the bloc.
High alert
Europe as a whole is on high alert after drone flyovers into NATO airspace reached an unprecedented scale last September, prompting European leaders to agree to develop a "drone wall" along their borders to better detect, track and intercept drones violating Europe's airspace.
In November, NATO military officials said a new US anti-drone system had been deployed to the alliance’s eastern flank.
And following a violation of Polish airspace, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the formation of the Eastern Sentry programme, which aims to deter further Russian incursions.
Some European officials described the incidents as Moscow testing NATO’s response, which raised questions about how prepared the alliance is against potential threats from Russia.
The Kremlin has dismissed allegations that Russia is behind some of the unidentified drone flights in Europe as "unfounded."

articles.title: Russia May Have Lost Two Key Kalibr Missile Carriers in Novorossiysk Strike
articles.body:
- Category

Russia May Have Lost Two Key Kalibr Missile Carriers in Novorossiysk Strike
Two Russian Black Sea Fleet frigates, Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen, reportedly sustained serious damage during an August 12 strike on the Novorossiysk naval base, according to Militarnyi on August 20, citing an analysis by the OSINT account Absolutely Reliable Source.
Satellite imagery released by the account appears to show damage to the frigates’ missile launch systems, raising the possibility that both vessels may have lost their ability to launch Kalibr cruise missiles. The exact extent of the damage has not been officially disclosed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi, Admiral Essen was hit in the bow section, deforming the deck and destroying an eight-cell module of the 3S14 universal vertical launch system used to fire Kalibr missiles.
The frigate’s Trebovaniye-M combat information and control system was also damaged.
Admiral Makarov, the flagship of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, was reportedly struck in the area of its vertical launch systems. According to the analysis, the impact caused an internal detonation and burned out the ship’s 3S14 launch cells.
The frigate also sustained damage to its radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems.
If the reported damage is confirmed, Russia’s Black Sea Fleet may have lost the operational use of two of its principal Kalibr missile carriers, the outlet reported.
Both vessels could also require extensive repairs if the damage to their launch systems is confirmed, with their return to combat service potentially taking at least a year, according to the assessment.
On August 12, Ukrainian forces launched an overnight strike against Russia’s naval base in Novorossiysk, targeting air defense positions, port berths, and other naval infrastructure, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy described the operation as unique, noting that Novorossiysk serves as Russia’s last major naval stronghold in the Black Sea and lies more than 300 kilometers from the frontline.

articles.title: Romania destroys a sea drone and finds aerial drone debris on its soil amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Romania destroyed an explosives-laden maritime drone near its critical Neptun Deep gas platform and recovered debris from a separate aerial drone that crashed on its soil, the Romanian Defense Ministry reported. The incidents came during a major Russian attack on Ukraine on 20 August that killed 14 people in Kyiv city and oblast, caused incidents in Moldova, and triggered air defense activation in Poland.
F-16 fires cannon at sea drone near gas platform
A commercial vessel spotted a drifting maritime drone near the Neptun Alpha production platform, approximately 80 nautical miles east of Constanța, at around 06:28, the Defense Ministry said. Two Romanian F-16s scrambled with orders to fire. One engaged the target with its onboard cannon—the first time Romania used a cannon against a drone and the first engagement against a maritime drone. All previous shootdowns used air-to-air missiles against aerial drones.
The country's Defense Minister Radu Miruță said the drone was carrying explosives and was spotted just hundreds of meters from the platform where several hundred people work. Through a recently established direct communication channel, Ukraine confirmed the drone was not of Ukrainian origin. President Nicușor Dan directly blamed Russia, condemning "the intensification of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation."
The engagement came nine days after Romanian navy divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting near the same platform by controlled detonation.
14 killed as Russia unleashes massive overnight barrage on unprotected Kyiv, striking homes, hospital, school and railway infrastructure
Aerial drone crashes in Romania's Tulcea County
Earlier overnight, Romanian radar detected aerial targets near the Ukrainian border at 02:23, the Defense Ministry said. Two Spanish F-18s from NATO's air policing mission and a Romanian IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter scrambled. At 03:21, a drone crossed into Romanian airspace 13 km east of Galați and crashed three minutes later near the village of Grindu in Tulcea County. No casualties or damage were reported. The fragments posed no explosive hazard.
The crash came four days after a Spanish F-18 shot down another drone over Romanian airspace, Euronews reported. Romanian F-16s intercepted three Russian drones in July.
Russian Shaheds hit near Moldova-border crossing, burn food cargo, and black out 13,000 in Odesa Oblast
Poland activates defenses, Moldova hit by drone spillover
Poland's Operational Command activated military aircraft and ground-based air defense systems during the Russian attack as a preventive measure. The Netherlands provided air defense support. No breach of Polish airspace was recorded.
Moldova faced multiple incidents. At 03:16, the country's National Army detected what was preliminarily identified as a Shahed-136/Geran-2 drone crossing from Ukraine near Kotlovyna in Odesa Oblast into Moldova's Gagauzia region. It returned to Ukrainian airspace six minutes later, public broadcaster Moldova1 said.
Separately, an explosion at a truck parking lot on Ukrainian territory about 150 meters from the Giurgiulești-Reni border crossing at around 03:45 sparked a fire that spread onto Moldovan soil, Newsmaker reported. Border police found drone fragments in a crater approximately 1 km inside Moldovan territory.

articles.title: "Darkness, night, everything on fire": Kyiv residents speak about Russia's latest attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
"Darkness, night, everything on fire": Kyiv residents speak about Russia's latest attack on Kyiv
Fifteen people were killed and 39 injured as a result of a Russian attack on Kyiv on the night of 19-20 August. Residents of damaged buildings have shared how they survived the night.
Source: Ukrainian public broadcasters Suspilne and Radio Liberty
Details: A multi-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district of Kyiv was damaged. The State Emergency Service is conducting search and rescue operations there.
Larysa, a resident of the destroyed building, told Suspilne that the explosions occurred shortly before midnight. Larysa lived on the fifth floor and the collapse occurred at the level of the seventh and eighth floors.
"It was very loud, it has never been this loud here. The last loud strike was the missile that hit the building. It caught fire, there was a blaze and destruction, and windows were blown out. People were panicking. Some were calling for their relatives, while others were in a state of complete shock. It was dark, night and everything was burning," Larysa said.
A neighbour of Larysa – a young man – was killed in the strike.
Olena, another resident of the building, said she hid with her family in the bathroom during the overnight attack. Their flat sustained significant damage, with the blast wave blowing out the doors.
"Everything in the flat went flying. The armoured door is lying right in the hallway. I hid in the bathroom with my child and my father. It was terrifying. We have no flat left, everything was blown apart. I just managed to hide my child in the bathroom," she said.
Another resident, Anastasiia, said she decided to go to a shelter early, so she was in a safe place during the attack. She said explosions could be heard in the shelter. Anastasiia then recognised her building from photos on social media and saw that it had been hit by a Russian missile.
"When the air-raid warning is issued, you don't have time to get to a shelter, and if you end up outside afterwards, it would mean certain death. We're not allowed back into our flats because it's too dangerous. But from the windows you can guess the scale of the destruction," she said.
Olha, another citizen affected by the Russian attack, was searching for a dog at the site of the attack – a border collie left with her by her son while he serves in the military.
"One bang. Two bangs. I was sitting in the kitchen. My son is at the front, his border collie is with me, and a cat too. I don't remember how I grabbed just my phone and ran into the corridor – the blast wave blew out the doors. I have two doors. We barely got out. She ran ahead of me and disappeared. I've been walking around looking for her the whole time," Olha told Radio Liberty.
Kyiv police officers told how they rescued a 51-year-old man. He was trapped under rubble after a ballistic missile strike on a warehouse. The man worked as a security guard.
Officers carefully extracted the man and carried him on a stretcher to a safe location. He was in a semi-conscious state and had numerous shrapnel and laceration wounds. He received medical treatment.
Background: On the morning of 14 August, nine-year-old Hlib Kovtunenko and his mother, 29-year-old Olha, were killed when Russia struck their home with two jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Drone attack reported on oil refinery in Russia's Perm
articles.body:
President Zelensky confirmed a drone strike on the Perm oil refinery over night. The strike in Russia's Perm Krai was reported early on Aug. 21 by Telegram media channels.
Videos shared by Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ purportedly show explosions and a fire in Perm, a city roughly 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine.
Exilenova+ said local residents reported a series of explosions at the refinery. OSINT analysts from ASTRA, an independent Russian Telegram channel, geolocated footage showing smoke rising near the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery.
Zelensky wrote on his Telegram channel, "We continue to use our long-range sanctions to return the consequences of the war to where it came from."
Local authorities warned residents of incoming unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) around 6.30 a.m. local time. Around the same time, temporary restrictions were introduced at Bolshoe Savino airport in Perm, ASTRA wrote. These have since been lifted.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down 325 Ukrainian drones overnight.
A previous attack on Jul. 29 struck the Lukoil-operated Perm oil refinery, one of Russia's largest.
Ukraine has intensified attacks on oil refineries and other energy facilities in Russia to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce revenues financing Moscow's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Companies of the "Rusal" group, Russian officials, and the creators of the animated series "Masha and the Bear" — who has been hit by Ukraine's new sanctions
articles.body:
Companies of the "Rusal" group, Russian officials, and the creators of the animated series "Masha and the Bear" — who has been hit by Ukraine's new sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine's new sanctions target Russian and Chinese companies, officials, collaborators, and the "Rusal" group. Restrictions have also been imposed on the creators of "Masha and the Bear".
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed four decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine on imposing sanctions against enterprises in Russia’s military-industrial complex, companies belonging to the sanctioned "Rusal" group, collaborators, senior Russian officials, and the authors and distributors of the animated series "Masha and the Bear," UNN reports, citing the Office of the President.
Details
Under one of the decisions, sanctions were imposed on 28 Russian citizens, 36 Russian companies, and one Chinese company. They include enterprises involved in supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, tools and components, electronics, and raw materials in circumvention of sanctions. Restrictions were also imposed on enterprises that manufacture and repair military and specialized equipment, conduct research in the field of drones, and develop specialized equipment and software for the needs of Russian security agencies.
Under another decision, Ukraine imposed sanctions on five enterprises of the "Rusal" group and nine Russian citizens associated with these companies. They are alumina importers and aluminum producers for the needs of Russia’s military-industrial complex. In circumvention of sanctions, nonferrous metallurgy enterprises also receive raw materials and provide products for the manufacture of military equipment, missile and artillery weapons, and military aircraft.
Under another decision, sanctions were imposed on 45 individuals and eight legal entities. They include senior Russian officials who justify and promote Russia’s armed aggression, the occupation of Ukrainian territories, and assist the Russian invaders, as well as entities serving Russia in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
In particular, sanctions were imposed on former lawmaker from the "Party of Regions" Yuriy Ivanyushchenko. He is a suspect in criminal proceedings concerning the legalization of land plots worth more than 160 million hryvnias. Enterprises associated with him also operate in temporarily occupied Crimea; he maintains ties with representatives of Russia’s criminal and business circles and has repeatedly visited russia since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Zelenskyy imposed sanctions on former MP Ivanyushchenko20.08.26, 23:05 • 230 views
"We continue to systematically identify and restrict the activities of enterprises working for Russia’s military-industrial complex. We expect our partners to support these efforts, and European companies to cease any interaction with such Russian enterprises, in particular with companies of the "Rusal" group. Sanctions must not only indicate involvement in Russia’s war machine, but also actually deprive it of resources and international ties," said Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Adviser and Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy.
Sanctions were also imposed on five Russians and four organizations involved in the creation and distribution of the animated series "Masha and the Bear," which spreads pro-Russian narratives disguised as children’s content, posing a threat to Ukraine’s national security.
From now on, the sanctions apply to the studio "Animaccord," which created the animated series, its founder, CEO, as well as the screenwriter, director and producer, the series co-author who pays funds into the budget of the aggressor state, and the owner of the rights to this propaganda cartoon.
"We must respond separately to Russian propaganda, especially when it is directed at children and distributed through major international platforms," Vladyslav Vlasiuk added.
Ukraine will provide partners with all the necessary information to synchronize sanctions in international jurisdictions.
To remind
As UNN reported, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed decrees on new sanctions against Russia’s military complex, and against those individuals who themselves became, in one way or another, part of the Russian way of life and maintain ties with this state despite even such a war.

articles.title: Russian Shaheds hit near Moldova-border crossing, burn food cargo, and black out 13,000 in Odesa Oblast
articles.body:
Russian strikes in southern Odesa Oblast overnight into 20 August left 13,000 utility customers without power, Odesa Oblast head Oleh Kiper reported. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said drones attacked a checkpoint on Ukraine’s border with Moldova.
Russia has intensified attacks on southern Ukraine’s Danube region, where ports and transport routes lie close to Moldova and Romania. The spillover from the attacks has forced these neighboring countries to close airspace, scramble aircraft, and shoot drones down.
The Odesa Oblast Military Administration said Russian strikes disrupted power in several communities, and repair crews began restoration work. It did not identify damaged electrical equipment or say whether the grid had been shut down as a precaution. Two truck trailers carrying food caught fire at another location, but firefighters extinguished both blazes, the State Emergency Service said. No casualties were reported.
Zelenskyy did not identify which crossing was attacked or describe the damage. The Izmail District State Administration later reported that Russia attacked the Reni community with Shahed-136 drones. It recorded a hit on an unspecified site near the Reni–Giurgiulești international checkpoint.
People and freight cross between Ukraine and Moldova through checkpoints such as Reni–Giurgiulești. The district administration did not describe the damage or say whether the checkpoint remained open.
Russian attacks keep reaching Moldova
At 03:16 on 20 August, surveillance systems operated by Moldova’s National Army detected an unauthorized flight, public broadcaster Moldova1 reported.
The object was preliminarily identified as a Shahed-136/Geran-2, a long-range explosive drone used by Russia. It crossed from Ukraine near Kotlovyna in southwestern Odesa Oblast and flew toward Etulia in Moldova’s autonomous Gagauzia region. It returned to Ukrainian airspace at 03:22.
Similar incidents occurred earlier in August. An unidentified aerial object exploded in a Moldovan field 12 kilometers from Ukraine on 9 August. On 17 August, Moldova closed part of its airspace for 15 minutes after Ukraine’s Air Force warned that a Russian Banderol, a jet-powered missile-drone, had crossed from Odesa Oblast. The object later exploded near Talmaza.
Romania activates defenses
On 20 August, Romania’s Defense Ministry said its radars detected targets near Ukraine at 02:23 and scrambled two Spanish F-18s and a Romanian helicopter. A drone entered Romanian airspace east of Galați at 03:21 and crashed near Grindu at 03:24. Its impact started a fire that went out on its own. Romania reported no casualties or material damage.
Four days earlier, a Spanish F-18 shot down a drone that entered Romania from Moldova. NATO said it appeared to be Russian.
Russia has recently intensified attacks on Ukraine’s Danube ports and struck the Mayaky bridge connecting southern Ukraine with Moldova and Romania. Such attacks can disrupt Ukraine’s transport links and force neighboring militaries to react within minutes.

articles.title: What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
Egypt's current absence from the collective security pact signed between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, dubbed the ‘Mecca Agreement’, has brought renewed attention to Egypt’s security strategy towards its regional allies and the wider region.
While speculation surrounding Egypt’s absence from the agreement abounds, understanding Cairo’s position requires looking beyond the Mecca Agreement.
Egypt’s regional security posture has historically been shaped by a preference for strategic flexibility, driven by the recognition that its interests often require maintaining relationships with competing regional and international actors.
Today, this approach is being tested by an increasingly volatile regional environment marked by state and non-state threats, from Israel’s expanding regional wars to the US-Israel-Iran war and its fallout.
The complexities of this geostrategic environment have compelled Cairo to emphasise diplomacy, mediation, and issue-based security cooperation over concrete, bloc-based alignments.
Its rapprochement with Turkey, expanding security ties with major regional players including Saudi Arabia, and maintenance of diplomatic backchannels with rival actors underscore Egypt’s efforts to diversify its security partnerships while preserving the flexibility to engage across regional fault lines.
Security through diplomacy
A 1955 telegram from the US Embassy in Cairo to the US Department of State documented a tense exchange between then Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser and then US Assistant Secretary of State George Allen over Egypt’s acquisition of Czechoslovak arms.
During the exchange, Nasser expressed doubts about Washington’s reliability as a security partner and raised concerns about Israel’s growing influence and territorial ambitions, particularly the influence of the Herut party, the predecessor to today’s Likud.
The exchange reflects a key feature of Egyptian strategic thinking. Cairo has long been sceptical of overreliance on a single external security umbrella, preferring instead to preserve room for manoeuvre.
That instinct remains salient in Cairo’s approach today. "Egypt has largely focused on managing and balancing its bilateral relationships with all major regional players to address growing instability and threats,” Liam Karr, Africa Team Lead at the Critical Threats Project, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s security is increasingly being tested by instability beyond its immediate borders, primarily driven by Israel’s expanding regional wars and now compounded by the US-Israel-Iran war. Previously assumed to be relatively shielded from these developments, Egypt has increasingly found itself directly exposed to their consequences.
Israel’s war on Gaza heightened Egyptian threat perceptions, particularly amid Israeli calls at the time for the displacement of Palestinians into Sinai, a scenario Cairo repeatedly identified as a red line.
The war also brought Israeli incursions closer to Egyptian territory. Throughout the war, Israel repeatedly asserted control over the Philadelphi Corridor, a narrow strip along the Egypt-Gaza border whose security arrangements have been shaped by the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty and subsequent agreements.
“Egypt’s threat perception has been shaped particularly by Israel’s unilateral security expansionism. This perception led to a greater emphasis on mediation across regional fault lines, while balancing against Cairo’s rivals, first and foremost Israel,” Ahmed Aboudouh, Associate Fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s response focused heavily on diplomacy. Alongside Qatar, Cairo maintained a central role in efforts to mediate between Israel and Hamas, positioning itself as an intermediary capable of communicating with multiple sides.
Earlier this month, US special envoy Jared Kushner met a Hamas delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, in a rare direct high-level meeting, to discuss implementation of the Board of Peace’s roadmap, namely the question of Hamas’s disarmament.
A durable end to the war on Gaza is vital to Egypt’s economic and security stability, particularly as the conflict continues to generate pressure along its border and across the Red Sea. Egypt’s economic vulnerabilities have raised the stakes. The Suez Canal, one of the country’s main sources of foreign currency, saw revenues collapse by roughly two-thirds at the height of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping.
The resumption of attacks on Red Sea shipping and rising regional tensions stemming from the US-Israel-Iran war further jeopardise Egypt’s economic security. Cairo also remains heavily reliant on Gulf investment and financial support, making stability across the Gulf and Red Sea increasingly inseparable from its own economic security.
The Egyptian economy has, however, shown some signs of recovery. In July, the IMF reinforced confidence in Egypt’s economic reform program, unlocking an additional $1.8 billion in funds after Cairo completed its latest review. That said, underlying vulnerabilities remain.
The widening geography of the US-Israel-Iran war was underscored in late July, when a drone struck Egypt’s Damietta port. The incident marked the first attack on Egyptian territory since the outbreak of the war, illustrating the interconnectedness of regional conflicts and directly exposing Egypt to new security threats. It also highlighted the urgency of reaching a durable resolution.
Egypt’s diplomatic leverage derives in large part from its ability to maintain relationships across divides. Earlier this year, Egypt used its diplomatic backchannel with the IRGC, an increasingly prominent decision-making actor in Iran, to help preserve a line of contact during a moment of heightened tension. Given the trajectory of regional dynamics, these channels are likely to remain important.
Egypt has also demonstrated a willingness to extend military support to its regional partners. During Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi’s visit to Abu Dhabi in May, he visited an Egyptian fighter detachment stationed in the UAE comprising Rafale jets and Egyptian pilots, alongside reports of Egyptian defensive deployments in Saudi Arabia.
Gulf security is closely aligned with Egyptian interests, but Cairo’s current absence from the Mecca agreement may reflect a recognition of the risks that a more hardened posture could invite, as well as a preference for maintaining strategic balance.
Issue-based cooperation over bloc alignment
Egypt maintains robust security relationships with all three members of the Mecca Agreement. Its current absence from the pact should therefore not be interpreted as a rejection of closer regional security cooperation.
Egypt and Turkey have considerably expanded their security cooperation as part of their broader political rapprochement. In June, the two countries conducted joint F-16 drills, the first exercise of its kind in almost two decades, building on the momentum generated by their 2025 joint maritime exercise, “Sea of Friendship.”
Ankara and Cairo have also pledged greater coordination on regional files including Sudan, Libya, and Gaza. Additionally, defence-industrial cooperation has expanded. Ankara and Cairo signed agreements worth approximately $350 million earlier this year aimed primarily at expanding joint production efforts.
These initiatives serve Egypt’s immediate defence needs while simultaneously enhancing regional strategic autonomy.
Cairo’s relationship with Riyadh is similarly deep. Egypt was among the 14 founding members of the Saudi-led Red Sea security maritime force. Its participation also builds on extensive experience in collective maritime security initiatives, including its current command, for the second time, of the Combined Maritime Forces’ Combined Task Force-153, the Red Sea focused task force.
“Egypt wants to be a central leader to regional approaches in its backyard, as shown by its involvement in the Sudan Quad, various multilateral security initiatives in the Red Sea, and the Libya and Palestine peace processes,” Karr told The New Arab.
Diversified partnerships
Participation in a formal collective security pact could strengthen deterrence, but it could also narrow Egypt’s room for manoeuvre and constrain its ability to mediate across regional divides.
“Egypt will maintain its cautious, defensive and risk-averse approach to avoid antagonising any party with leverage to pressure its direct national interests,” said Aboudouh.
Egypt will likely continue diversifying its security partnerships rather than committing to formal blocs. In line with this posture, China and Egypt are currently hosting the second iteration of their joint aerial exercise, "Eagles of Civilisation," from mid-August to early September, following the inaugural exercise held in 2025.
Strategically, Cairo will also have to guard against military overstretch as it manages simultaneous pressure across two turbulent fronts, the Middle East and the Nile Basin. Ethiopia's plans for three additional dams on the Nile have already drawn strong opposition from Cairo.
Managing these competing pressures will reinforce Egypt’s preference for diversified partnerships and strategic flexibility, allowing it to deepen cooperation where its interests converge while avoiding overreliance on any single security partner.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options

articles.title: Air defense downs 107 of 135 Russia targets; 27 strike UAVs hit 16 locations
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Forces intercepted 107 Russia targets overnight into Friday; however, hits by 27 strike UAVs were recorded across 16 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense shot down/neutralized 107 Russia UAVs of the Shahed type, Gerber, and other drone types in the north, south, and east of the country," the statement said.

articles.title: Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
articles.body:
Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
At the same time, one of the most dangerous potential scenarios is the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against a NATO member state and a Chinese operation against Taiwan. Ukrainian diplomat Ihor Dolhov expressed this view in his program “Ihor Dolhov’s Program,” which was released on Ukrinform’s YouTube channel.
He noted that Ukraine possesses Patriot anti-aircraft missile launchers but currently faces a shortage of missiles to counter Russian ballistic attacks. According to Dolhov, the problem with stocks of such missiles is not limited to Ukraine. “There are fewer of them in the United States. There are fewer of them in Europe. There are fewer of them in other countries,” the diplomat noted.
Dolhov attributes this situation, in particular, to the extensive use of American weapons during the Gulf War.
At the same time, Russia continues its massive attacks on Ukraine and is striking Ukrainian ports, creating additional risks not only to the country’s security but also to its economy. According to Dolhov, Russian strikes have significantly hampered exports through Black Sea ports, and a further blockade of Ukrainian agricultural exports could have consequences for global food security. “A humanitarian crisis, a food crisis due to a shortage of wheat and grains on the market. Russia is also threatening to freeze Ukraine out this winter,” the diplomat noted.
He emphasized that, at the same time, the international security situation is deteriorating: Russia is escalating its threats against European countries and Japan, while the war in the Middle East is diverting a significant portion of U.S. military resources.
According to Dolhov, this creates additional opportunities for China to increase pressure around Taiwan.
The diplomat cited the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against one of the NATO member states and a Chinese operation against Taiwan—as one of the most dangerous potential scenarios. “And NATO will have no means to respond. Nor will the United States be able to help either Europe or Taiwan. They will be completely tied up in the war in the Persian Gulf,” Dolhov stated.
According to him, under such conditions, Europe must focus not only on finding a new format for negotiations but, above all, on strengthening its ability to deter Russia and compel it to engage in genuine negotiations.
Earlier, The Atlantic reported that NATO leadership is taking increasingly seriously the scenario of a simultaneous attack by Russia on Europe and by China on Taiwan. At the same time, the U.S. and NATO are not prepared for a simultaneous war with Russia and China.

articles.title: MQ-9 Lost in Middle East Last Year Due to Chafed Wire: New Report
articles.body:
A frayed wire likely triggered stray voltage to shut off a fuel valve, causing the catastrophic loss of an MQ-9 Reaper drone last August, according to a new Air Force investigation report.
The aircraft, valued at $23.6 million, was destroyed in place. It is among at least 40 MQ-9s lost or shot down over the past 18 months.
Air Combat Command released the Accident Investigation Board report on Aug. 13, nearly a year after the Aug. 31, 2025, mishap. The exact location of the mishap was not disclosed—the report said only that it took place in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility.
The MQ-9 belonged to the 432nd Wing at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., while the pilot and sensor operator were from the 89th Attack Squadron at Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D. The drone was returning from a mission to its base in the region and had been in the air nearly 19 hours when the engine shut off.
The drone automatically attempted to restart the twice, and the crew tried two manual restarts as well before the Reaper crashed to the ground. Operators tried for a soft landing to preserve the aircraft but were not successful.
After sorting through several options to avoid population centers and minimize damage, the crew selected a “relatively flat and isolated” piece of desert and tried to go in with the landing gear down, according to the report. But the crew lost contact with the aircraft as it descended below 2,000 feet.
The Reaper landed near the selected landing area, but “the force of the impact caused its landing gear to collapse,” according to the report. “Following the landing, sensitive equipment was removed from the [aircraft] and the remaining wreckage was demolished on site.”
The problem occurred on the aircraft’s first flight after its engine was replaced as part of a routine 3,000-hour engine inspection. During that inspection, personnel from contractor Honeywell noted three issues beyond normal wear:
- The propeller governor cable was chafed and replaced
- The fuel control unit was replaced with a new unit overhauled in April 2025, due to a missing log card
- The compressor seal was leaking and replaced
Notably, the inspection and replacement routine did not include removing the top cover from the fuel control unit, which regulates the flow of fuel to the engine—despite “known examples of the FCU sensor wire chafing,” according to MQ-9 manufacturer General Atomics. Honeywell personnel reported they had observed “a relay wire shorting and sparking” while servicing a different aircraft.
Based on data logs, investigators determined the MQ-9 engine experienced a spike in fuel flow just before plummeting to zero. General Atomics was able to recreate that sequence in its lab by suddenly closing the electrical fuel shutoff valve.
Those tests, combined with the known issue of the wires chafing inside the fuel control unit, led investigators to conclude the most likely explanation for the mishap was that a frayed wire inside the fuel control unit leaked enough voltage to trigger the fuel shutoff valve to close.
The board noted that while most U.S. Air Force aircraft are required to undergo some sort of check flight after their engine is replaced “to ensure the aircraft is airworthy and to test the flight integrity of all systems, particularly critical systems like those affecting engines,” the MQ-9 maintenance manual has no such requirement, the board said.
What’s more, investigators noted with surprise that a complete engine change is considered “routine maintenance” on MQ-9s, and that the crew controlling the drone was never informed that their aircraft had just received an entirely new engine.
The Accident Investigation Board cited inadequate planning and briefing and inadequate written standards as “relevant factors” in the mishap.
MQ-9 Losses
The MQ-9 mishap occurred during a relative lull in operations in the Middle East. Just months earlier, from March to May 2025, Operation Rough Rider sought to halt attacks on commercial shipping by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Houthis downed about a half dozen MQ-9s during that stretch using electro-optical/infrared surface-to-air missile systems, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
At least two dozen MQ-9s were subsequently lost during Operation Epic Fury against Iran starting in late February, some to air defense missiles and some struck on the ground.
By May, after a brief ceasefire took hold, the Air Force was down around 30 Reapers, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Hostilities began again in earnest by July, and the Washington Post reported last week that “at least 45” MQ-9s have been destroyed.
The Air Force reported having 230 MQ-9s in its inventory at the start of fiscal 2025; one year later, it had just 182. In May, Lt. Gen. David Tabor, Air Force deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, said the fleet was down to around 135 aircraft.
Air Force officials have praised the performance of the MQ-9 in the Iran conflict, saying it has accounted for many of the thousands of strikes conducted during the campaign and gathered valuable intelligence. Some have also hinted that commanders have sometimes employed them in ways that put the drones at greater risk.
With the fleet shrinking, leaders are discussing how to replace the losses. Options include acquiring the few remaining MQ-9As from General Atomics, buying the larger MQ-9Bs now being built, or developing replacement platforms. Among the alternatives backed by some on the Air Staff is a project jointly pursued by the Defense Innovation Unit and the Air Force. The so-called “massed modular aircraft,” or MMA is conceived as an “attritable” aircraft whose loss is treated more like a munition than a aircraft. Vendors have offered proposals and an acquisition official said in July that one or competitors could be selected by the end of 2026.

articles.title: Russia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger Japan
articles.body:
Japan has criticised missile tests carried out by Russia’s navy around the disputed islands visited by Vladimir Putin last week amid continuing tensions between the two countries.
Russia’s Pacific fleet said on Thursday that it had fired Bastion surface-to-ship missiles from Etorofu, the largest island in the disputed archipelago, simulating an attack on enemy vessels, hitting all of its targets approximately 300km away.
Officials said the drills included a nuclear-powered submarine and a guided-missile cruiser, according to reports.
Putin sparked a tit-for-tat summoning of ambassadors in Tokyo and Moscow with his first visit last week to Etorofu, the largest of the group of four islands. They are referred to as the Northern Territories or Four Northern Islands in Japan, and as part of the Kuril Islands in Russia.
Toshimitsu Motegi, Japan’s foreign minister, said on Thursday during a trip to Oman: “We cannot tolerate moves to strengthen military power on the Four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].”
Territorial rows over the islands go back to the 19th century. The Soviet Union seized them from Japan at the end of the second world war.
Exercises by the Russian fleet began on 4 August and Japan was informed in advance that they would include live-fire drills. Japan lodged a protest against the large-scale manoeuvres on 5 August.
According to the Russian news agency Tass, the drills involved “approximately 60 surface ships, submarines, and support vessels, about 30 aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial systems of the Pacific fleet’s naval aviation, as well as over 13,000 service members”.
Putin observed some of the exercises from the Varyag on 12 August as part of his trip to the disputed islands and to Sakhalin, the large undisputedly Russian island north of Hokkaido.
“The region is unfortunately becoming increasingly prone to conflict, with Nato seeking to gain a foothold here and the emergence of new military and political blocs,” said Putin, speaking aboard the flagship. “There are efforts and plans to deploy new weapons systems here, which creates threats for our country.”
The Russian drills are scheduled to continue through 29 August.

articles.title: Romania destroys drone near offshore gas project, blames Russia

A Romanian F-16 fighter jet on Aug. 20 destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project, with Romania's president blaming Russia for the latest incident involving the NATO member bordering Ukraine.
Unauthorized drone activity has become increasingly frequent in recent months across eastern European countries as Ukraine fights off a Russian invasion launched in 2022, with both countries increasingly relying on drone warfare.
In the latest incident, the drone that was destroyed was "loaded with explosives" and did not originate from Ukraine, Defense Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook.
"I strongly condemn the escalation of such irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation," Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on X.
The drone was spotted at 6:28 am local time (0328 GMT) by a commercial vessel, hundreds of meters from the offshore gas project Neptun Deep and 80 nautical miles east of the Black Sea city of Constanta, according to a press release from the defense ministry.
Two Romanian F-16 aircraft were deployed to respond, and one of them destroyed it.
Hundreds of people are currently working at Neptun Deep, according to the government. Neptun Deep is due to start production in 2027.
NATO has shot down four aerial drones in Romania recently, with the latest incident happening during last weekend.
The eastern European country also reported an aerial drone crash on Aug. 20 following Russian strikes on Ukraine.
It fell in an unpopulated area four kilometers (2.5 miles) northeast of the village of Grindu in eastern Romania, close to the border.
No casualties were reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Aug. 20 urged a global response to Moscow's "escalation" of the four-year war after Russian bombardments killed at least 16 people in Kiev and surrounding areas overnight.

articles.title: 'We will tear you to pieces': Indian general warns Erdogan about pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan
articles.body:
Retired Indian Maj.-Gen. Gagan Deep Bakshi warned that the growing alignment among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan could pose a strategic threat to India, while stressing that New Delhi would not sacrifice its ties with Iran to accommodate Israel’s security concerns.
Speaking to the New Delhi-based network, Republic World, Bakshi argued that the emergence of what he calls a "Sunni NATO" in the Middle East is a source of strategic concern for India.
At the same time, he sent a clear message to Israel: The alliance between the two countries is important, but New Delhi will not give up its interests with Iran simply because of the war between Jerusalem and Tehran.
According to Bakshi, the agreement that took shape in Mecca among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has created a new regional reality from India's perspective. "A Sunni NATO comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has been established in the Middle East, in Mecca, and that is a serious cause for concern," he said.
Bakshi stressed that, from India's perspective, Shi'ite Iran serves as an important counterweight to Pakistan.
Iran as a counterweight to Pakistan
"We very much need Shi'ite Iran to be on our side because Pakistan is our primary security headache. China may be the main threat, but together with it, Pakistan is our biggest security headache," he said.
Bakshi compared the threat Iran represents in Israel's eyes with that posed by Pakistan from India's perspective.
"Iran does not have even a single nuclear bomb, and yet it is perceived as an existential threat to Israel. And what about Pakistan? A fundamentalist, jihadist Islamic state that possesses 180 nuclear warheads," he claimed.
He added that India had not seen Israel display similar concern over Pakistan's nuclear arsenal.
"We have not seen Israel losing sleep over the bombs in Pakistan's hands because they are considered a threat only to India," he said.
According to Bakshi, the rapprochement between Ankara and Islamabad is not merely theoretical. He cited Turkish assistance to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, claiming that Turkey supplied it with nearly 1,000 unmanned aerial vehicles and helped operate them.
"This was already a 'Sunni NATO,' with or without an agreement. Turkey and Pakistan are already in an undeclared practical alliance," he said.
Bakshi also noted that during the confrontation, Turkey sent a warship to the port of Karachi, arguing that this was another expression of the close security ties between the two countries.
"Turkey has the largest army in NATO," he said, while questioning its ability to intervene directly in a war between India and Pakistan because of the geographical distance.
According to Bakshi, any Turkish force attempting to come to Pakistan's aid would have to travel through the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian Sea.
"The Indian Navy can tear apart any Turkish armada that tries to come to Pakistan's aid," he said.
India will not sacrifice its interests with Iran
A central part of Bakshi's remarks was directed squarely at Israel. He stressed that India views Israel as a friend, but would not agree to subordinate its own interests to Israeli needs, particularly when it comes to Iran.
"I am afraid that at some point Israel will also have to be sensitive to Indian concerns," he said. "We are not the 51st state of the United States, and for that matter we are also not an appendage or client state of Israel. We are friends, certainly. But vassals? No, sir."
"You cannot simply whistle and make our senior leaders go here and there, and ask us to sacrifice our interests," he said.
Bakshi specifically addressed possible pressure on India to distance itself from Iran because of the war.
"You cannot tell us: Throw Iran away because you are at war with it. When it comes to Iran, you cannot ask us to sacrifice our interests."
According to Bakshi, relations with Iran are vital to India economically and geostrategically as well. He pointed to the possibility of purchasing Iranian oil at low prices, refining it at Indian refineries, and subsequently exporting the products to other markets.
Beyond that, he stressed Iran's importance as an overland route for India.
"Iran provides India with the land bridge to Central Asia and the land bridge to Afghanistan, and these are of vital importance to us."
India cannot afford to give up those routes because of the war between Israel and Iran, he said.
"We cannot close these land routes because Israel is at war with Iran."
Bakshi concluded that the friendship between India and Israel remains important, but that from New Delhi's perspective, it has clear limits when major security and economic interests are at stake. Against the backdrop of growing ties between Turkey and Pakistan, and Indian concerns over a broader Sunni alliance, he believes that India's relationship with Iran is becoming more important, not less.

articles.title: The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
articles.body:
The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was reportedly offered a plan in early 2026 to launch large-scale drone strikes against airports in Moscow and Moscow Oblast.
Source: The Atlantic, citing two people familiar with the situation
Quote: "Early this year, Ukrainian officials came to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a risky new plan to end the war with Russia. It would require expanding their bombing campaign to include a set of targets and a class of weapons they had long avoided."
Details: According to two sources cited by The Atlantic, officials proposed expanding Ukrainian strikes to Moscow's airports using drones equipped with artificial intelligence. The aim would have been to disrupt the operations of international airlines flying to and from the Russian capital.
If conducted, the plan would have been unprecedented in the history of warfare. It envisaged swarms of autonomous drones equipped with AI-based navigation systems independently locating and striking targets without being controlled by an operator.
According to the journalists, similar systems have been tested by various countries, including the US, in recent years. Meanwhile, the legality of their use is the subject of an ongoing debate because of the potential for violations of international humanitarian law. No country has yet used such systems in combat.
The Atlantic reported that the plan was presented to Zelenskyy in the winter. The Ukrainian president expressed serious concern about the potential threat to civilian aviation, including the risk of accidentally striking a passenger aircraft or killing civilians near the airports.
Despite these concerns, Zelenskyy, seeking a way to put pressure on Russia and revive the peace process, allowed preparations for such strikes to continue for some time, The Atlantic said.
The Atlantic reported that by mid-spring, preparations had progressed sufficiently far and the project had been given the name M&M's.
The Atlantic said former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov played a key role in the project. According to the sources, he was involved in assembling a team of developers, developing AI-based guidance systems and seeking funding to produce large numbers of autonomous UAVs.
However, preparations for the operation were subsequently halted.
A representative from the Office of the President of Ukraine denied the information in comments to The Atlantic, calling the claims false.
There is currently no official confirmation that such a plan was developed or existed.
Background:
- Moscow and Moscow Oblast have come under repeated drone attacks in recent months. For example, on the night of 18-19 August, Russian authorities again reported a drone attack on Moscow.
- On the night of 17-18 August, the Russian authorities reported that more than 600 drones were heading towards Moscow.
- On the afternoon of 18 August, Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that more than 1,600 drones had been shot down over a 24-hour period, along with 10 guided aerial bombs and two HIMARS rockets.

articles.title: Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria, denies military presence in air base
Turkey “will not fall into the trap” set by Israel, the country’s presidency said in a statement, days after Tel Aviv struck the Abu al-Duhur air base located near Aleppo.
"We are experienced enough not to fall into the trap of figures like (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu, who aim to undermine peace and stability in our region," said Burhanettin Duran, the Turkish presidency's director of communications.
After the site was struck, causing damage to its runways, reports said that a Turkish delegation had been at the site just hours earlier, but Turkey has denied a military visit to the location.
Israeli media said a Turkish military delegation had been at the site, and a Syrian monitor said the delegation was there as part of efforts to rehabilitate the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Turkish forces had recently toured the base, warning that Israel would not tolerate a "threat" from a Turkish presence there.
"We will not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment moving southward, because it threatens us," Netanyahu told an army radio podcast.
The premier's office also said on Tuesday evening that Israel had repeatedly warned Syria that deploying Turkish forces at an airbase near Aleppo would pose a threat to its national security, noting that Damascus had ignored the warnings.
The office stated that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the status quo on security matters, claiming that Damascus was on the verge of violating this understanding by allowing the Turkish military deployment.
But Turkish defence ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said the strikes were "unacceptable" and that Ankara would act "resolutely" to protect Syria's efforts to establish post-war stability.
"Israel's attack on the Abu al-Zuhur air base is aimed at harming Syria's stability, security, unity, integrity and infrastructure. Attacks violating Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable," he told journalists.
"In this context, our efforts and contributions to protect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and help it establish a stable and secure environment, will continue resolutely."
Turkey’s presidency has also clarified that it is not considering retaliation.
Duran said that Netanyahu was "clinging to this irrational stance due to upcoming elections, internal political tensions, and fears. He views hostility toward Turkey as a political lifeline".
The development comes as Syria’s new transitional government has condemned the Israeli strikes, which marked the first time the location was targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.
The US has also rebuked the strikes, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Agencies contributed to this report.

articles.title: FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
articles.body:
FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
Russian security officers have detained a foreign national suspected of surveilling critical infrastructure sites on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence, the Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Friday.
The suspect was taken into custody this month in Murmansk Region near the border, as he sought to illegally cross into Norway, the agency said in a statement. The detained man is believed to have a longstanding relationship with Kiev’s special services, having voluntarily contacted them back in 2023 for the first time, according to FSB.
The man’s Ukrainian handlers had ordered him to travel to Moscow and conduct reconnaissance at a key train hub “to identify freight trains transporting petroleum products, as well as administrative buildings in the city center,” the FSB said. He was involved in an “attempt to launch an FPV drone” to gather the intelligence, it added.
The Kiev regime has intensified attempts to stage terrorist attacks in Russia to compensate for the mounting pressure it has been experiencing on the frontline, as well as its inability to inflict “meaningful damage on critical infrastructure sites in Moscow Region,” the agency warned. The planned attacks involve short-range kamikaze drones that were supposed to be launched from an immediate vicinity of targeted sites by planted agents and local collaborators recruited online, including victims of fraudulent Ukrainian call centers, the FSB said. Involvement in such activities incurs heavy penalties under Russian law, up to life behind bars, the agency stressed.
Last month, the FSB said it had thwarted a major Ukrainian FPV drone plot, which involved smuggling 24 AI-guided drones into the country and using them to target a key defense industry enterprise and military airfields. The failed operation had been prepared by Kiev’s intelligence with the direct involvement of Western handlers, the agency said at the time.
The disassembled drones had been flown into Russia using fixed-wing UAVs and balloons, which were collected by the suspects and transferred deeper into the country for assembly and preparations for the attack. However, the whole operation had been closely monitored by Russian secret services from the very beginning, and the perpetrators and their accomplices ended up in custody.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
articles.body:
US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, the U.S. military said Thursday, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the U.S. or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month.
The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defense for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented.”
Hegseth spoke with the Lincoln’s crew last week, and Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited this past weekend. In an editorial published Sunday by The Wall Street Journal, Cooper said the crew “delivered a performance for the ages, and now you are going home.”
Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. While renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran calmed in recent weeks, the Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war.
Hegseth has said the U.S. can maintain the blockade “indefinitely.”
President Donald Trump this week downplayed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its homeport in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. Trump called the nearly nine months at sea that the sailors endured a “good period of time” but added that “over the years, we’ve had them out there much longer.”
Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with a retired admiral over the weekend who recounted being on ships for “much longer.” Trump said the admiral assured him that the Lincoln is “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” Trump did not name the admiral.
In a statement Sunday after visiting the Lincoln, Cooper praised the carrier’s leaders for prioritizing mental health and resilience.
“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper said.
The Washington joins the USS George H.W. Bush in the Middle East, leaving Asia without an American carrier strike group at a time when China has shown more signs of aggression.
The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: Pirates hijack cargo ship carrying Turkish weapons off Somalia’s coast, official says
articles.body:
Pirates hijack cargo ship carrying Turkish weapons off Somalia’s coast, official says
MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Pirates hijacked a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship off Somalia’s Puntland coast earlier this week and took the vessel, which was carrying Turkish weapons, toward the region’s Nugaal coast, a Somali official said Thursday.
The M/V LUTUF was seized on Monday about 3½ nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district, the official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity, because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about sensitive information.
The ship, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu, as well as communications and satellite equipment, the official said.
The 10-member crew included six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards, he said.
There was no immediate comment from Turkish authorities about the incident.
Eight pirates, believed to be members of a group previously involved in the hijacking of the M/V Sward on April 26, took the vessel toward the coast near Garmaal in Puntland’s Dangoroyo district.
Two Turkish-owned vessels later approached the hijacked ship, while Turkish helicopters and drones monitored the area, the official said. On Tuesday, a small boat carrying two men approached the vessel and delivered khat, a stimulant commonly chewed in Somalia, he said.
After the boat returned to shore, an airstrike followed, killing four men and wounding two others, the official said.
The circumstances of the strike, including who carried it out and whether those killed were involved in the hijacking, couldn’t immediately be independently verified. The status of the LUTUF, including its crew and cargo, wasn’t immediately clear. The AP couldn’t independently verify all details of the account.
___
Suzan Fraser contributed to this report from Ankara, Turkey.

articles.title: She made sushi last year—now she flies combat drones for Ukraine’s army
articles.body:
Khrystyna, 22, joined Ukraine's 159th Separate Mechanized Brigade after finding the unit on social media and leaving her contact details — a recruiter called her back and offered her the "18–24" contract, she said in a video published on the brigade's Facebook page.

A drone operator track added in July 2025 extends the commitment to two years and includes up to 45 days of basic training and up to 60 days of professional drone training.

The Unmanned Systems Forces—established in June 2024 as the world's first military branch dedicated to unmanned systems—number about 15,000.

articles.title: Norway Expands Finnmark Brigade With Artillery and Air Defense
articles.body:
Norway has established three new units within the Finnmark Brigade: an artillery battalion, a combat air defense battery and a communications company.
The Norwegian Armed Forces reported this.
The Norwegian Army says the accelerated formation of the brigade is linked, among other factors, to the deteriorating security situation in Europe. The new structure is intended to strengthen Norway’s military presence in Finnmark, the country’s northernmost region.
The Finnmark Brigade’s artillery battalion is being equipped with K9 VIDAR self-propelled howitzers, Norway’s version of the South Korean K9 Thunder.
The first four K9 VIDAR systems, along with support vehicles, have already arrived at the Garrison of Porsanger.
In 2025, the Norwegian government separately proposed allocating NOK 17 billion to develop the Army. Of that amount, NOK 5.6 billion was earmarked for the procurement of 24 K9 self-propelled howitzers to fully equip the Finnmark Brigade’s artillery battalion.
The K9 VIDAR can engage targets at ranges of more than 40 kilometers. In the future, the system is planned to use ramjet-powered ammunition, which could increase its effective range to more than 120 kilometers.
The formation of the artillery battalion is currently progressing faster than initially planned. The Norwegian Army expects the main conditions for its deployment to be in place by 2028.
The Finnmark Brigade is scheduled to be fully operational by 2033. It will then have around 4,000 personnel, including career soldiers, conscripts and reservists.
When the brigade was established in 2025, it had 280 permanent personnel. Their number is expected to increase to around 350 in fall 2026 and to 700-800 by 2033.
Finnmark Brigade commander Brig. Gen. Jon Olav Fuglem said the creation of the new units has already strengthened the military presence in the region. At the same time, the brigade needs new barracks, housing, offices and other infrastructure for further expansion.
Late last year, Norway announced plans to significantly strengthen its 198-kilometer border with Russia. The plans included new fencing, modern surveillance systems and drones for aerial monitoring.

articles.title: Russia faked broadcasts from Sweden’s national TV to smear its PM—the same network already hit Germany and France this month
articles.body:
Russia's Matryoshka bot network has launched disinformation campaigns targeting elections in Sweden, Germany, and France this month, fabricating video clips branded with the logos of trusted European media outlets, Sweden's national public broadcaster SVT reported. Analysts in multiple countries found the campaign aims not to reach mass audiences but to overwhelm newsrooms' fact-checking capacity.
Fake clips target Swedish PM weeks before the vote
Seven fabricated video clips appeared on the social media platform X within a single hour on 18 August. Among them were clips branded with the logos of SVT and the Swedish newspaper Dagens Nyheter. Others hijacked the visual branding of Euronews and Germany's Der Spiegel. None were ever produced by these outlets.
The fake videos spread lies about election fraud in Sweden and directed false accusations at Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson personally. Sweden holds general elections on 13 September.
"We see this all over Europe. Russians target countries that support Ukraine," Kristersson told SVT.
Russian opposition analysis group Antibot4navalny linked the posts to Matryoshka, a pro-Russian influence campaign named after the Russian nesting doll.
Also known as Operation Overload and Storm-1679, Matryoshka was first exposed by Antibot4navalny in 2024 and is one of several Kremlin-linked disinformation networks alongside the Doppelgänger campaign and Storm-1516. A previous SVT review found the majority of Matryoshka's posts aimed to influence Western support for Ukraine.
Sweden says it stopped Russian operation to discredit country and EU. But no one will be prosecuted
Campaign targets newsrooms, not audiences
The fabricated posts rarely get more than a few hundred or a few thousand genuine views, Antibot4navalny told SVT. Analysts say the campaign is not primarily designed to reach a large audience. Matryoshka operators actively push fabricated posts to journalists and fact-checkers, often disguising them as verification requests. A 2024 report by France's state anti-disinformation body Viginum suggested the campaign aims to distract and overload newsrooms' fact-checking resources through large volumes of targeted requests. In posts targeting Sweden, the network tagged the social media accounts of several outlets, including SVT and Dagens Nyheter.
The campaign may also seek to generate media coverage that amplifies its message or makes it appear more influential than it is, the think tank ISD assessed.
Sweden detains Russians who “camped” near home of CEO of Gripen jets Ukraine is buying
Germany and France targeted the same month
On 12 August, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), warned that Matryoshka is targeting local and regional elections in Germany scheduled for September. In early August, France's Viginum detected a Matryoshka operation directed at presidential candidate Gabriel Attal ahead of the 2027 vote. French prosecutors opened a probe into the campaign on 18 August.
In April, the network promoted false claims of Ukraine's involvement in the assassination attempt on US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: A year after recognising Palestine, Britain faces calls to act
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
On anniversary of 'symbolic' Palestine recognition, UK groups demand end to Israel arms trade
With the first anniversary of Britain's official recognition of the State of Palestine approaching, six British pro-Palestinian organisations have stepped up pressure on the government, calling for an end to the arms trade with Israel, the suspension of military and intelligence support, and comprehensive sanctions against it.
The demands come alongside calls for British action that goes beyond political recognition to practical measures.
In a comment to The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, Chris Nineham, vice-president of the Stop the War Coalition, said Britain's recognition of Palestine "was welcome, but, as we feared, it was symbolic", adding, "The people of Palestine need action, and we are calling on our government to end British support for Israel immediately.
"We are working to organise another mass demonstration on 10 October to pressure it to take action."
Nineham's comments come as the organisations prepare to organise a new national march in central London next October, in an attempt to pressure the British government to take tougher steps towards Israel.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the organisations said that "Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face killing, hunger and displacement, while British-funded humanitarian aid remains subject to Israeli restrictions".
They called on the British government to work to halt Israeli attacks and ensure aid reaches the Strip without restrictions.
The demand to lift restrictions on aid coincides with a position Britain announced at the UN Security Council on 11 August, when it called on the Israeli authorities to end what it described as "unacceptable restrictions" on aid and allow safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.
'Britain must act'
The statement is titled, "Three years of genocide... Britain must act".
The signatories said their next march will take place on Saturday, 10 October, at noon in central London, coinciding with three years since the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The official website of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign confirms the date and location of the march.
The statement was signed by the Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the Stop the War Coalition, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Friends of Al-Aqsa, and the Muslim Association of Britain.
The United Kingdom officially recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025.
At the time, the government said that the decision aimed to revive hope for peace and a two-state solution.
But the organisations that signed the statement believe the recognition was not followed by British action at the required level.
They say "real action" requires ending arms trade with Israel and suspending military and intelligence support that they consider to contribute to facilitating violations of international law.
They also called for British companies, banks, universities and charities to be prevented from supporting activities linked to the occupation or settlements, starting with a ban on trade connected to Israel's illegal occupation and extending to comprehensive sanctions against Israel.
Britain suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after concluding that there was a clear risk that the equipment covered by them could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
The latest government data shows that six additional licences were subsequently suspended or amended as new information emerged.
The organisations expanded their demands to include the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, warning of continued settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The British government, for its part, says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
It recently condemned the rise in settler violence and expressed concern about developments at the Noble Sanctuary in Jerusalem.
In June, London, in coordination with international partners, imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual, saying they were involved in financing, enabling or carrying out acts of settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Britain also strengthened its guidance for British companies and citizens in June, explicitly advising them against engaging in economic or financial activities in Israeli settlements, which it considers illegal, while reaffirming its continued support for trade with Israel within its pre-1967 borders.
In their statement, the organisations said Britain's commitment to international law "cannot be held hostage to the Israeli electoral timetable", arguing that the time had come to move from political recognition of the Palestinian state to practical measures.
The organisers are calling for widespread participation in the 10 October march, in an attempt to put pressure back on the streets of Britain.
They also want to place the issues of arms, sanctions, trade and military support at the forefront of the debate over what has actually changed in British policy since the recognition of Palestine.
